What you'll learn

  • Install VS Code and Git on your own computer.
  • Confirm the install by running git --version in VS Code's terminal.
  • Create a free GitHub account with a username you won't regret later.

By the end of this course you will have done what working developers do many times a week: written down a problem, fixed it on a branch, opened a pull request, answered a reviewer's comments, and merged the result into a shared project. Everything you need for that is free. It comes down to three programs, and each has one job.

#Three tools, three jobs

Tool Where it lives Its job
Git Your computer Records the history of a project folder: every saved version, who made it, and why.
GitHub A website (github.com) Hosts a shared copy of that history and adds teamwork features: pull requests, reviews, and issues.
VS Code Your computer The editor where you write files. It has a terminal and a Source Control panel that talk to Git.

People mix up Git and GitHub all the time. Git works with no internet connection and no account. GitHub is one popular place to share what Git records, the way a photo-sharing site is a place to share photos your camera took.

#Before you start

  • You need a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Chromebook that allows Linux apps. Phones and tablets won't work.
  • You need permission to install software. School-managed laptops often block this, so try it early and tell your instructor if you get stuck.
  • GitHub's terms say you must be 13 or older to have an account (older in some countries). If you're younger, all of Module 2 works without an account, and you can follow the GitHub parts with an adult or your instructor.
  • Set aside about 30 minutes. Install VS Code first, because the Git installer for Windows looks for it.

#Step 1: Install VS Code

Windows

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab) and click the Windows button. This downloads the User Installer, which doesn't need an administrator password.
  2. Run the installer and accept the license.
  3. On the Select Additional Tasks screen, leave Add to PATH ticked. Ticking the two Open with Code boxes is handy too: you'll be able to right-click a folder and open it in VS Code.
  4. Finish the installer and open VS Code once.

macOS

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab) and click the Mac button.
  2. Open the downloaded .zip if your Mac didn't unzip it automatically, then drag Visual Studio Code.app into your Applications folder. Running it from Downloads causes update problems later.
  3. Open VS Code from Applications.
  4. Press Cmd+Shift+P to open the Command Palette, type shell command, and run the command that installs code in your PATH. Now you can type code . in a terminal to open the current folder.

Chromebook

  1. Turn on Linux first: open Settings, go to About ChromeOS, then Developers, and click Set up next to Linux development environment. Accept the defaults and wait a few minutes.
  2. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab) and download the .deb file for your Chromebook's chip (x64 for Intel or AMD, Arm64 for ARM).
  3. In the Files app, drag the .deb from Downloads into Linux files.
  4. Open the Terminal app and install it:
  1. Find Visual Studio Code in the launcher's Linux apps folder.

#Step 2: Install Git

Windows

  1. Go to git-scm.com/install/windows (opens in a new tab) and click the download link for the latest version. Most PCs need x64 Setup; laptops with ARM chips (such as Snapdragon) need ARM64 Setup.
  2. Run the installer. It has many screens; the defaults are fine except for two:
    • Choosing the default editor used by Git: pick Use Visual Studio Code as Git's default editor. The default is Vim, which confuses almost every beginner.
    • Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories: choose Override the default branch name for new repositories and type main. GitHub uses main, so this keeps you consistent.
  3. Keep the recommended choices on the other screens, including Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software and Git Credential Manager. That last one handles signing in to GitHub in the next lesson.
  4. The installer also adds Git Bash, a terminal that understands the same commands as Mac and Linux. You'll use it in VS Code below.

macOS

  1. Open Terminal (press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter).
  2. Type this and press Enter:
  1. If a version number appears, Git is already installed. If a box pops up saying the git command requires the command line developer tools, click Install and wait for it to finish (it can take 10 minutes). You can also start that install yourself with xcode-select --install.
  2. If you already use Homebrew (opens in a new tab), brew install git gets you a newer version. You don't need Homebrew for this course.

Open VS Code and choose Terminal > New Terminal from the menu bar. A terminal panel opens at the bottom. Type:

💡 Tip

Windows users: VS Code's terminal opens PowerShell by default. Switch it to Git Bash so the commands in this course work exactly as written. Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run Terminal: Select Default Profile, and pick Git Bash. Then close the terminal and open a new one.

#Step 4: Create your GitHub account

  1. Go to github.com/signup (opens in a new tab).
  2. Enter your email address, a password, and a username, then solve the puzzle GitHub shows you.
  3. Type the code GitHub emails to you. Choose the Free plan if asked.

Your username shows up in every link to your work, like github.com/your-username/project. Choose something you'd be comfortable showing a teacher or putting on a college application in three years. If you'd rather stay private, leave your full name and birth year out of it. GitHub may also ask you to turn on two-factor authentication; it's worth doing, and an authenticator app on your phone is the easiest way.

#What usually goes wrong

  • git: command not found, or on Windows 'git' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet. The terminal was opened before Git finished installing, so it doesn't know where Git lives. Close VS Code completely, reopen it, and open a new terminal. If that fails, restart the computer.
  • On a Mac, xcrun: error: invalid active developer path. A macOS update removed the developer tools. Run xcode-select --install again and accept the prompt.
  • No Linux option on a Chromebook. Your school or family account has turned it off. Ask your instructor about another computer before the first session.
  • You picked Vim by mistake on Windows. No need to reinstall. The next lesson sets VS Code as Git's editor with one command.

⚠️ Watch out

Only download Git from git-scm.com and VS Code from code.visualstudio.com. Search ads for "free Git download" sometimes lead to look-alike sites that bundle unwanted software.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Tell Git your name and a private GitHub email so every commit is labeled correctly.
  • Set main as the default branch name and VS Code as Git's editor.
  • Connect your computer to GitHub with an SSH key or a credential manager.
  • Prove the setup works by cloning a real project and reading its history.

Every commit you make carries a name and an email address, and once a commit is shared, that label travels with it. Make your first commit with your personal email, push it to a public project, and anyone who downloads that project can read the address. Ten minutes of setup avoids that, and it's the same setup professionals do on every new laptop.

Do all of this in VS Code's terminal (Terminal > New Terminal). On Windows, use the Git Bash profile you chose in the last lesson.

#Step 1: Use GitHub's private email address

GitHub gives every account a "noreply" address that links commits to your profile without revealing your real inbox.

  1. On GitHub, click your profile picture (top right), then Settings.
  2. In the Access section of the sidebar, click Emails.
  3. Tick Keep my email addresses private. GitHub now shows your noreply address, which looks like 12345678+yourname@users.noreply.github.com. Copy it.
  4. Also tick Block command line pushes that expose my email. If you ever forget and commit with your real address, GitHub will refuse the push instead of publishing it.

#Step 2: Tell Git who you are

Replace the name and email with yours (keep the quotes):

These commands print nothing when they work. Ask Git to read the name back to check:

--global means "for every repository on this computer, for my user account". Without it, the setting applies only to the repository you're standing in, which is how you'd use a different email for one school project.

📝 Note

user.name is a label, not a login. It doesn't have to match your GitHub username, and Git never checks it. Use the name you want people to see next to your work.

#Step 3: Two defaults that prevent confusion

The first makes every new repository start on a branch called main, matching GitHub. The second tells Git to open VS Code whenever it needs you to type a longer message. The --wait part makes Git pause until you close that tab, so it knows you've finished writing.

Now list everything you've set:

Git stores these in a plain text file called .gitconfig in your home folder. Running a git config command again with a new value simply overwrites the old one, so typos are easy to fix.

#Step 4: Choose how your computer proves it's you

Reading a public project from GitHub needs no login. Sending your work to GitHub does. GitHub stopped accepting your account password from Git years ago, so you need one of two methods:

  • HTTPS with a credential manager. The first time you push, a browser window asks you to sign in to GitHub. The credential manager stores a token securely so you never type it again.
  • An SSH key. You create a pair of matching keys. The private key stays on your laptop; the public key goes on GitHub. When you connect, your laptop proves it holds the private key without ever sending it.

Both are secure. The tabs below give the simplest route for each computer.

Windows (HTTPS)

Nothing to do yet. The Git installer already set up Git Credential Manager. The first time you push in Module 3, a sign-in window appears; choose to sign in with your browser and approve the request on the GitHub page that opens. After that, pushes just work.

Prefer SSH? Follow the Chromebook steps in Git Bash; they work the same on Windows. To paste your public key, use cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | clip to copy it.

macOS (SSH)

  1. Create a key, using your noreply email as its label. Press Enter to accept the default file, then type a passphrase (the screen stays blank while you type, which is normal):
  1. So you don't retype the passphrase every time, create ~/.ssh/config (run touch ~/.ssh/config, then code ~/.ssh/config) and paste:
  1. Add the key to the Mac keychain, then copy the public key:
  1. On GitHub: profile picture > Settings > SSH and GPG keys > New SSH key. Give it a title like "MacBook", leave the type as Authentication Key, paste into Key, and click Add SSH key.

Chromebook (SSH)

  1. In the Linux Terminal, create a key. Press Enter for the default file and type a passphrase:
  1. Print the public key and copy the whole line it shows (it starts with ssh-ed25519):
  1. On GitHub: profile picture > Settings > SSH and GPG keys > New SSH key. Name it "Chromebook", paste the line into Key, and click Add SSH key.

If you used SSH, test the connection:

The first time, SSH asks whether you trust github.com and shows a fingerprint. GitHub publishes its fingerprints; for the modern key type it's SHA256:+DiY3wvvV6TuJJhbpZisF/zLDA0zPMSvHdkr4UvCOqU. If yours matches, type yes. Then you'll see:

That "does not provide shell access" part is GitHub's normal greeting, not an error. Your username in the message is the proof.

⚠️ Watch out

The file without .pub (id_ed25519) is your private key. Never paste it into GitHub, a chat, or an AI tool. If you think it leaked, delete it from GitHub's SSH keys page and generate a new pair.

#Step 5: Prove it works with a real repository

Make one folder to hold every project in this course, then clone GitHub's practice repository into it:

clone downloaded the project and its entire history. Look at both:

The first three lines are files. The last three are commits, newest first: a short ID, then the message someone wrote. The labels in parentheses show where your copy and GitHub's copy currently point; Module 3 explains them. You'll be writing lines like these in the next module.

#What usually goes wrong

  • Permission denied (publickey). GitHub didn't find a matching public key. Check that you pasted the .pub file's contents, all on one line, and that the key shows on your SSH and GPG keys page.
  • Host key verification failed. You pressed Enter or typed no at the fingerprint question. Run ssh -T git@github.com again and type yes.
  • Git opens a strange editor full of ~ symbols. That's Vim, which means core.editor isn't set. Type :q! and press Enter to escape, then run the core.editor command from Step 3.
  • code: command not found when Git opens the editor. On a Mac, run the Command Palette's shell command from the last lesson so the code command exists.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Which file do you paste into GitHub's New SSH key box?

  • That's the private key. It must never leave your computer.

  • The public key is safe to share. GitHub uses it to check answers signed by your private key.

  • That file holds your name and email settings, not a key.

Show answer

B. The public key is safe to share. GitHub uses it to check answers signed by your private key.

2You ran git config --global user.email with a typo. What's the fix?

  • Far more than needed; you'd lose your other settings too.

  • git config overwrites the old value, so the newest command wins.

  • Git never checks. It stamps whatever you typed onto every commit.

Show answer

B. git config overwrites the old value, so the newest command wins.

  • GitHub Docs: Connecting to GitHub with SSH (opens in a new tab): the official steps for every OS, including passphrase tips.
  • GitHub Docs: Caching your GitHub credentials in Git (opens in a new tab): how Git Credential Manager and the GitHub CLI handle HTTPS sign-in.
  • Pro Git: First-Time Git Setup (opens in a new tab): what each git config level means.

What you'll learn

  • Keep every course project in its own folder, and check which repository you're in.
  • Find your way around VS Code's Source Control view and match its buttons to Git commands.
  • Follow four privacy rules before anything goes on GitHub.
  • Recover from the error messages and "stuck" screens beginners see most often.

Git's error messages look alarming, but most of them tell you exactly what to type next. Look at what Git prints when you ask about a folder that isn't a repository yet, and when you forget to stage a file:

The first says Git looked in this folder and every folder above it for a hidden .git folder and found none. The second ends with the fix in parentheses. Reading the whole message, slowly, solves more problems than searching online.

#One folder per project, all inside git-course

You made ~/git-course in the last lesson. Every project in this course gets its own folder inside it, and each of those folders becomes its own repository:

A repository is just a folder with a hidden .git folder inside it. That .git folder is the history; delete it and the files stay but the history is gone. To check which repository you're in, ask Git for its top folder:

Run the same command somewhere that isn't a repository and you get the not a git repository error from above. That's useful too: it means you're not about to commit into the wrong project.

⚠️ Watch out

Never run git init in your home folder, Desktop, or Documents. Git would treat every file in it as part of one giant project, and git status would list thousands of files. If it happens, the fix is to delete only the hidden .git folder at the top of that folder (for your home folder: rm -rf ~/.git). Your files stay; only the accidental tracking goes away. Check with your instructor before deleting anything if you're unsure.

Also keep git-course outside OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Google Drive, and Dropbox. Sync apps copy files while Git is writing to .git, which can leave a repository in a broken state. Once you push to GitHub in Module 3, you'll have an off-computer copy anyway.

#A tour of VS Code's Source Control view

Open a repository folder with File > Open Folder…, then click the branching icon in the left bar (or press Ctrl+Shift+G). You'll see:

In VS Code What it means Same as
Changes list Files you've changed but not staged git status
Letter U, M, or D Untracked (new), Modified, Deleted git status
+ next to a file (Stage Changes) Put this file in the next commit git add file
− in Staged Changes Take it back out git restore --staged file
Message box and Commit button Save a snapshot with that message git commit -m "…"
Curved arrow (Discard Changes) Throw away your edits to that file git restore file
Branch name in the bottom-left status bar Which branch you're on; click to switch git switch
Colored bars beside line numbers Green: added, blue: changed, red marker: deleted lines git diff

This course teaches each idea with terminal commands first and then shows the button. The commands are worth learning because every Git tool, website, and tutorial uses the same words. Once you know what git add does, the + button stops being mysterious.

#Privacy and safety rules for this course

Anything in a public repository can be read, copied, and archived by anyone. Git also remembers every version, so deleting a file in a later commit doesn't remove it from history. Four rules keep you safe:

  1. Never commit secrets. No passwords, API keys, access tokens, or .env files. If one slips into a commit that's been pushed, treat it as public: change the password or delete the key on the site that issued it first, then clean up the repository.
  2. Keep personal details out. Your noreply email is already set. Don't put your address, phone number, school schedule, or photos of yourself in READMEs or commit messages.
  3. Make practice repositories private if you'd rather nobody sees them. Private repositories are free on GitHub, and you can make one public later.
  4. Don't paste commands you don't understand, especially ones with --force, rm -rf, or sudo. Ask what a command does before you run it, whether the suggestion came from a forum or an AI tool.

On GitHub, be the collaborator you'd want: comment on the work, not the person. If someone is rude or harassing, use the … menu on their comment to report it, and tell your instructor.

#Accessibility settings worth knowing

  • Zoom VS Code with Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- (Cmd on a Mac), or pick a High Contrast theme with Ctrl+K Ctrl+T.
  • Screen readers: VS Code switches to Screen Reader Optimized mode when it detects one. In a diff, press F7 to open the Accessible Diff Viewer, which reads changes line by line. Alt+F1 (Option+F1 on Mac) opens accessibility help for whatever you're focused on.
  • Red and green are hard to tell apart? Git's colors are settings. These two lines make removed lines magenta and added lines blue:
  • On GitHub, press ? on most pages to list keyboard shortcuts. Settings > Accessibility lets you underline links and stop animated images from playing.

#A routine for getting unstuck

When something goes wrong, work through these in order:

  1. Run git status and read every line, including the hints in parentheses. It tells you the branch, what's staged, and what Git expects next.
  2. Read the last line of the error. Lines starting with fatal: or error: name the actual problem.
  3. Check the command's options with -h. For example, git restore -h starts like this:
  1. Ask for help with three things: the exact command you ran, the full output (copy it as text, not a blurry photo), and what you expected to happen.

#Screens that look frozen

  • git log fills the screen and shows : or (END) at the bottom. You're in a pager that lets you scroll. Use the arrow keys, and press q to quit.
  • A screen full of ~ characters appears. Git opened Vim. Press Esc, type :q!, and press Enter. Then set core.editor as in the last lesson.
  • A command is still running and you want out. Press Ctrl+C.

#Errors you'll probably see this month

fatal: pathspec 'indx.html' did not match any files: a typo in a file name. Run ls to see the real names, or press Tab to autocomplete them.

Author identity unknown: Git doesn't know your name and email yet.

Run the two git config commands from the last lesson (with your noreply email), then commit again.

nothing added to commit but untracked files present: you ran git commit before git add. Stage the file first. Module 2 explains why Git makes you do both.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1git log printed a long list and the bottom line shows (END). The terminal won't take new commands. What do you do?

  • That works, but it's slow, and nothing is broken.

  • You're in a scrolling pager; q quits it and returns you to the prompt.

  • There's no such command, and the pager would just treat the keys as scrolling input.

Show answer

B. You're in a scrolling pager; q quits it and returns you to the prompt.

2A classmate's tutorial tells you to commit a file called .env so the project "just works" for everyone. What's the problem?

  • Size isn't the issue; they're usually tiny.

  • Once pushed, a secret should be treated as public. Share a template like .env.example with fake values instead.

  • It can; .gitignore itself starts with a dot and is committed in almost every project.

Show answer

B. Once pushed, a secret should be treated as public. Share a template like .env.example with fake values instead.

  • VS Code: Accessibility (opens in a new tab): every zoom, contrast, keyboard, and screen reader option in one page.
  • GitHub Docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository (opens in a new tab): what to do if a secret does reach GitHub.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what a commit stores and why each one has a long ID.
  • Move changes from the working tree to the staging area to the repository with git add and git commit.
  • Read the output of git status, git diff, and git log.
  • Write commit messages someone else can understand, and undo uncommitted changes with git restore.

A group project lands in your shared drive looking like this:

Which one is newest? What changed between final-2 and final-final-2, and who changed it? Was the chart removed on purpose? The folder can't answer any of that. Git replaces the pile with one set of files plus a list of labeled snapshots, each saying what changed, who changed it, when, and why.

#What a commit actually stores

Think of a save point in a video game that also makes you write a note: "beat the boss, low on health". A commit is a save point for a project folder.

More precisely, each commit records:

  • a snapshot of every file Git is tracking, exactly as they were at that moment,
  • the author's name and email and the time,
  • a message describing the change,
  • a link to its parent, the commit that came right before it.

Git names each commit with a 40-character ID (a hash) calculated from all of that, such as 449ccec1b2bd7d5beb7d2de9575441160c108d81. Change one letter in a file or the message and the ID comes out completely different, which is how Git notices tampering or corruption. You'll usually see just the first seven characters, 449ccec, which is enough to identify it.

#Three places your work lives

Here's the part that confuses most beginners. Saving a file in VS Code doesn't put it in Git's history. A change passes through three places:

  1. Working tree: the files in your folder, the ones you open and edit.
  2. Staging area (also called the index): a waiting area for the next commit. You choose what goes in.
  3. Repository: the committed history, stored in the hidden .git folder.

Why not commit straight from your folder? Because you're often in the middle of two things. Say you fixed a typo in the README and you're also halfway through a new page. Staging lets you commit just the typo fix now, with a clear message, and keep working on the page.

#Watch one file make the trip

Make a folder called recipes inside git-course, open it in VS Code, and run git init in its terminal. That creates the hidden .git folder. Then create pancakes.md with a short ingredient list and ask Git what it sees:

Untracked means Git can see the file but has never recorded it. Stage it and check again:

The heading changed to Changes to be committed: the file is in the staging area. Now commit, with a message after -m:

That first line packs in a lot: the branch (main), the fact that this is the very first commit (root-commit), the short ID, and your message. Run git status now and it says nothing to commit, working tree clean, meaning your folder matches the last snapshot exactly.

#See what changed with diff and log

Edit the recipe: change 2 eggs to 1 egg and add a line for salt. Then:

Lines starting with - were removed and lines starting with + were added. A changed line shows up as one of each. The @@ -1,5 +1,6 @@ line says "this chunk covers 5 lines starting at line 1 in the old version, and 6 lines in the new one". Lines with a leading space are unchanged context, there to help you find your place.

🧪 Try it yourself

Run git add pancakes.md, then predict what git diff prints. Run it to check, then try git diff --staged.

Plain git diff compares your working tree to the staging area. Once you stage everything, there's no difference, so it prints nothing. git diff --staged compares the staging area to the last commit, which is exactly what you're about to commit. Checking it before every commit is a good habit.

Commit that change, then look at the history:

Newest commits come first. (HEAD -> main) marks where you are now. For a compact view, use git log --oneline, and to see exactly what one commit changed, use git show followed by its ID.

#Messages your future self can read

Six months from now, git log --oneline is how you'll find the commit that broke something. Compare:

Unhelpful Helpful
stuff Add pancake recipe
fixed it Fix negative total when cart is empty
changes Use one egg and add salt
Updated index.html Link the events page from the home page

A few conventions most teams share:

  • Start with a verb in the command form: Add, Fix, Remove, Rename. A handy test: the message should complete the sentence "If applied, this commit will ___."
  • Keep the first line short, around 50 characters, with no period at the end.
  • If the why isn't obvious, add a body. A second -m becomes a separate paragraph: git commit -m "Use one egg" -m "Two made the batter rubbery."
  • One idea per commit. "Fix typo and redesign the menu" should be two commits.

#Undo changes you haven't committed

git status already showed the tool for this, in its hints. Two commands cover most situations:

This throws away your edits and puts the file back the way it was at the last commit (or the staged version, if you'd staged it). It's how you recover when you've made a mess of a file and want a clean start.

This takes the file out of the staging area but keeps your edits in the folder. Use it when you staged something by mistake.

⚠️ Watch out

git restore pancakes.md deletes uncommitted work for good. There's no recycle bin, because Git never recorded those edits. If you might want them later, commit first or copy the file somewhere safe.

#Common mistakes

⚠️ Watch out

Editing a file after staging it. git add stages the file as it was at that moment. Edit it again and git status lists the same file twice:

If you commit now, the newer edits are left out. Run git add pancakes.md again to stage the latest version.

⚠️ Watch out

Running git add . without looking. The dot means "everything in this folder", including junk files and anything private. Run git status first and read the list. The next lesson shows how .gitignore keeps junk out for good.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You run git add notes.md, then type two more lines into notes.md and save, then run git commit -m "Add notes". What does the commit contain?

  • The staging area holds the version from the moment you staged it. The two new lines are still only in your working tree.

  • Saving a file never changes the staging area; you'd need to run git add again.

  • Git commits the staged version without complaint and leaves the newer edits as unstaged changes.

Show answer

A. The staging area holds the version from the moment you staged it. The two new lines are still only in your working tree.

2Right after git add pancakes.md, git diff prints nothing. Why?

  • If git add failed, it would print an error.

  • It works any time; it just compares two specific places.

  • Use git diff --staged to compare the staging area to the last commit.

Show answer

C. Use git diff --staged to compare the staging area to the last commit.

3Which is the most useful commit message?

  • Every commit updates files. This says nothing about what or why.

  • Which thing? This won't mean anything in a month.

  • It starts with a verb, names the specific problem, and fits on one short line.

Show answer

C. It starts with a verb, names the specific problem, and fits on one short line.

4You staged secret-notes.txt by mistake but want to keep the file in your folder. Which command?

  • For a file that has never been committed, that does nothing useful; for a committed file, it would throw away your edits.

  • This unstages the file and leaves it untouched in your working tree.

  • The file would then be in history forever.

Show answer

B. This unstages the file and leaves it untouched in your working tree.

Key takeaways

  • A commit is a snapshot of every tracked file, plus author, time, message, and a link to its parent.
  • Changes move from the working tree to the staging area with git add, and into history with git commit.
  • git status tells you where every changed file is; git diff and git diff --staged show the exact lines.
  • Good messages start with a verb and say what changed and, when it isn't obvious, why.
  • git restore --staged unstages; git restore discards uncommitted edits permanently.

#Further reading

  • Pro Git: Recording Changes to the Repository (opens in a new tab): the official book's chapter on status, add, diff, and commit, with more examples.
  • How to Write a Git Commit Message (opens in a new tab): Chris Beams's widely shared guide, with the reasoning behind each convention.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a project folder into a repository and keep junk out of it with .gitignore.
  • Make focused commits, staging one file at a time when two changes are unrelated.
  • Check every change with git diff before committing it.
  • Rescue a broken file with git restore.

You're going to build the website for a school robotics club and give it a history that someone joining the club next year could read and trust. The site is tiny on purpose; the point is the history. This same project carries on through Modules 3 and 4, where it gets branches, pull requests, issues, and reviews.

Here's the page you'll end up with:

And here's the history behind it, four commits that each do one thing:

#Step 1: Create the project files

In VS Code's terminal:

A new VS Code window opens on the empty folder. Create these three files with File > New File and save each one:

Real project folders also collect things that don't belong in history. To see that happen, make a drafts folder with a file of private ideas in it. On a Mac, Finder quietly creates a .DS_Store file in folders you open; on Windows, File Explorer sometimes makes Thumbs.db.

#Step 2: Turn the folder into a repository

Git sees five things (on Windows or a Chromebook you probably won't have .DS_Store). Three are the website. .DS_Store is Mac clutter that would show up as noise in every future git status, and drafts/ holds notes you don't want published. If you typed git add . now, both would be in history permanently.

#Step 3: Write a .gitignore before the first commit

A .gitignore file lists patterns for files Git should pretend it can't see. Create it in the project's top folder:

Lines starting with # are comments. A plain name matches that file anywhere in the project, and a trailing / matches a folder and everything in it. Now ask again:

The clutter and the drafts are gone from the list, and .gitignore itself appears. You do commit .gitignore, so everyone who works on the project gets the same rules. If you're curious what's being hidden, git status --ignored lists it.

#Step 4: Make the first commit

The list now holds only what belongs in the project, so git add . is safe:

#Step 5: Add a change, and record why

New members keep asking when the club meets. Add one line to index.html, under the first paragraph:

Before committing, read the diff to make sure it says only what you meant:

One + line and nothing else, which is exactly the change you intended. This time the reason is worth recording, so give the commit a body with a second -m:

#Step 6: Two unrelated changes, two commits

Now make two edits before committing anything. In style.css, color the heading:

In README.md, add a section telling people how to preview the site:

These have nothing to do with each other, so they deserve separate commits. The short form of status makes the staging visible:

Each line has two columns before the file name: the left column is the staging area and the right column is the working tree. M means "modified, not staged" and M means "modified and staged". After git add style.css, only the CSS moved to the left column. Commit it, then stage and commit the README:

If the color turns out to be a mistake next month, you can undo that one commit without touching the README.

💡 Tip

In VS Code's Source Control view, this step is just two clicks: hover over style.css in Changes, click +, type the message, click Commit. Then repeat for README.md.

#Step 7: Rescue a broken file

Accidents happen. Suppose a bad paste wipes out the bottom half of index.html and you save it. git diff --stat gives a quick summary of the damage:

Seven lines gone, none added. Since the last commit had the good version, bring it back:

The file is exactly as it was at the last commit. This is the everyday payoff of committing often: the last commit is always a safe place to return to.

#Step 8: Read the history you made

Read it bottom to top and it's the story of the project. To see the reason you recorded in Step 5, show that commit:

Your IDs and dates will be different, because IDs come from your name, the time, and the content.

#The finished project

Four files are tracked, and two things are deliberately ignored:

Keep club-site exactly where it is. In Module 3 you'll put it on GitHub and add a new page on a branch.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why write .gitignore before the first commit instead of after?

  • .gitignore only affects untracked files. Anything already committed stays in history, so it's easiest to keep junk out from the start.

  • You can add or edit .gitignore at any time.

  • Order doesn't matter to Git; it reads the file whenever it checks status.

Show answer

A. .gitignore only affects untracked files. Anything already committed stays in history, so it's easiest to keep junk out from the start.

2In Step 6, why stage style.css and README.md separately?

  • A commit can include any number of files, as Step 4 showed.

  • One idea per commit keeps the log readable and lets you reverse the color change without losing the README section.

  • Git doesn't care about file types or order.

Show answer

B. One idea per commit keeps the log readable and lets you reverse the color change without losing the README section.

3git status --short shows M style.css (M in the left column). What does that mean?

  • That would be M, with the M in the right column.

  • The left column describes the staging area, so the change is ready to commit.

  • There are no branches or merges yet; M here just means modified.

Show answer

B. The left column describes the staging area, so the change is ready to commit.

Key takeaways

  • Write .gitignore before your first commit, and commit the .gitignore itself.
  • Read git diff before every commit to catch changes you didn't intend.
  • Give each commit one idea; stage files separately when you've made unrelated changes.
  • Add a message body with a second -m when the reason for a change isn't obvious.
  • git restore returns a file to its last committed version, which makes frequent commits a safety net.

#Extend it

  • Add a projects.html page listing two robots the club has built, linked from index.html. Commit the new page and the link as one commit, since one makes no sense without the other.
  • Make a change, stage it, then decide you don't want it in this commit. Use git restore --staged and confirm with git status --short.
  • Open the Source Control Graph in VS Code's Source Control view and click each commit to see its changes.

  • GitHub's gitignore templates (opens in a new tab): ready-made .gitignore files for Python, Node, Java, Unity, and dozens more.
  • Git documentation: gitignore (opens in a new tab): the exact pattern rules, including *, **, and ! for exceptions.

What you'll learn

  • Decode git status --short output at a glance.
  • Rewrite vague commit messages and split mixed work into focused commits.
  • Write and test a .gitignore, and stop tracking a file that was committed by mistake.
  • Choose the right undo command, search history for a change, and amend the last commit.

Make a folder called practice inside git-course and give each exercise its own small repository inside it (mkdir the folder, cd into it, git init). They're throwaway, so experiment freely. Your commit IDs will differ from the ones shown here.

#Warm-up: read the short status

A classmate runs git status --short and gets this:

For each file, say whether it's untracked, staged, unstaged, or some mix. Remember: the left column is the staging area and the right column is the working tree.

Show solution
  • about.md: modified, not staged (M on the right only).
  • contact.md: modified and staged (M on the left only).
  • faq.md: both. Some edits were staged, then the file was edited again. Committing now would leave the newer edits out.
  • news.md: a new file, staged (A for added).
  • todo.md: untracked. Git has never recorded it.

#Exercise 1: Rewrite the messages

These are real-looking messages from a group project. Rewrite each so it starts with a verb and says what changed. Invent reasonable details.

Need a hint?

Use the test "If applied, this commit will ___." A reader should be able to guess the diff from the message alone.

Show solution

Many answers work. What matters is a specific verb and a specific thing:

Before After
stuff Add photo gallery page
fixed bug Fix score resetting when the game restarts
asdf Remove test text from the footer
Updated style.css Increase body text size for readability
final version!!! Add conclusion section to the report

Notice that "Updated style.css" names the file but not the change; Git already records which files changed, so the message should say what and why.

#Exercise 2: One messy afternoon, two commits

Make a repository called study-notes with biology.md containing Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the sell. and commit it. Now, without committing in between, (a) fix the typo "sell" to "cell", and (b) create chemistry.md with one line of notes. Commit these as two separate commits with good messages.

Your git log --oneline should end up with three commits.

Need a hint?

Stage one file, commit, then stage the other. git status --short before each commit shows what's going in.

Show solution

The typo fix shows as 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-): Git sees a changed line as one line removed and one added.

#Exercise 3: Write a .gitignore for a Python project

A weather-bot folder contains:

Write a .gitignore so that git status shows only .gitignore, bot.py, and example.env. Then prove each rule works with git check-ignore -v, which prints the rule that matched a file.

Need a hint?

You need four patterns. One of them uses * to match any file ending in .log, wherever it is. Be careful that your .env rule doesn't also hide example.env.

Show solution

Each line shows the file, the line number in .gitignore, and the pattern that caught it. The pattern .env matches only a file named exactly .env, so example.env stays visible, which is what you want: it shows other people which settings exist without revealing the real key. Running git check-ignore -v example.env prints nothing, meaning no rule matches.

#Exercise 4: Stop tracking a file that was already committed

In a game-scores repository, someone committed settings.local.txt (personal settings that differ per computer). You add settings.local.txt to .gitignore, edit the file, and run git status --short:

Git still reports changes to it. Explain why, then fix it so the file stays on your computer but is no longer tracked.

Need a hint?

.gitignore only applies to files Git isn't already tracking. You need to remove the file from the staging area (and so from the next snapshot) without deleting it from your folder. git rm has an option for "only from the index".

Show solution

.gitignore doesn't affect files that are already in a commit, so Git keeps watching it. Remove it from tracking with --cached, which leaves your copy alone:

"Deleted" here means deleted from the next snapshot. Commit it together with the .gitignore:

The file is still in your folder, and future edits to it won't appear in git status. The old commit still contains it, though. If the file had held a password, you'd also need to change that password.

#Exercise 5: Two kinds of undo

In a poems repository with two committed files, you've done two things you regret: you typed asdfjkl over all of haiku.txt and saved it, and you staged a half-finished edit to limerick.txt. git status shows:

Get haiku.txt back to its committed version, and unstage limerick.txt while keeping your limerick edits.

Need a hint?

The hints in parentheses in that output contain both answers. One command takes an option and one doesn't.

Show solution

limerick.txt is back to M: modified but unstaged, with your edits intact. haiku.txt no longer appears because it matches the last commit again.

#Exercise 6: Find when something changed

Build a band repository with schedule.txt and four commits: add the schedule (Tuesday, 4:00 pm, Room 101), move practice to Thursday, add a README, then change the time to 4:30 pm and the place to the music room. Now pretend you forgot all that. Use Git to answer: which commit stopped mentioning Room 101, and what else did it change?

Need a hint?

git log -S "some text" lists only the commits that added or removed that exact text. Then git show with an ID shows that commit's full diff.

Show solution

Two commits touched the text: the one that added it and the one that removed it. Show the newer one:

It also moved the time from 4:00 to 4:30. Another useful view is git log --oneline -- schedule.txt, which lists every commit that touched that one file and skips the README commit.

#Challenge: Fix the commit you just made

In a mixtape repository, you commit with a typo in the message and forget to include a new file:

Fix both problems so the history shows one commit with the right message and both files, not a second "oops" commit.

Need a hint?

git commit --amend replaces the most recent commit with a new one built from the staging area. Stage the missing file first.

Show solution

The bad commit 27f7a06 is gone from the log and d040155 replaces it with both files. The ID changed because the content and message changed.

Only amend commits you haven't pushed yet. Once a teammate has a copy of a commit, replacing it rewrites history they depend on; make a new commit instead.

What you'll learn

  • Explain a branch as a movable name for a commit, and HEAD as "the branch you're on".
  • Create, switch, merge, and delete branches with git switch and git merge.
  • Predict whether a merge will fast-forward or create a merge commit.
  • Describe how origin, push, and pull connect your repository to GitHub, and what a pull request adds.

The robotics club's website is live, and main is what visitors see. Two people want to change it: Priya is building an events page that will take a week, and Marcus is adding a dark mode. If they both commit half-finished work straight to main, visitors get a page that says "EVENTS: TODO" in dark gray on black. Branches fix this. Each person works on their own line of history, and main changes only when a piece of work is finished and checked.

#A branch is a name stuck on a commit

The intuition: a branch is a sticky note with a name on it, stuck to one commit. Making a new branch doesn't copy any files; it just adds another sticky note. When you commit, the sticky note for the branch you're on moves forward to the new commit.

Precisely: a branch is a tiny file inside .git that holds one commit ID. HEAD is another file that says which branch you're on. You can look at them yourself in the recipes repository from Module 2:

git branch lists branches and stars the current one. HEAD points at main, and main is literally a file containing the ID of the newest commit. That's the whole trick, and it's why branches in Git are instant and cheap.

Step through this small Python model of the same idea. branches maps names to commits, head is the branch you're on, and every commit moves only the current branch:

Notice that when C is committed, main stays on B. The final line is a fast-forward merge: nothing new is created, a name just slides forward.

#Make a branch and work on it

git switch -c creates a branch and switches to it in one step:

Create waffles.md, stage it, and commit. Then look at the log:

The labels tell the story: you're on add-waffles, one commit ahead, and main still points at the older commit. Now switch back:

waffles.md vanished from your folder. Don't panic: it's safely stored in the add-waffles commit. Switching branches rewrites your working tree to match the commit that branch points at. Switch back and the file reappears.

📝 Note

Branch names can't contain spaces. Short, lowercase, hyphenated names that describe the work are the norm: add-events-page, fix-footer-year. Avoid names like sam-stuff that say nothing about the change.

#Bring the work back with git merge

To merge, switch to the branch you want to receive the work (usually main), then name the branch to merge in. There are two possible outcomes.

#Fast-forward: main hadn't moved

Since you branched, nobody committed to main. So Git doesn't need to combine anything; it can slide main forward to the waffle commit.

After a fast-forward, history is a straight line again, and main and add-waffles point at the same commit. The branch has done its job, so delete the name (the commits stay):

#Merge commit: both sides moved

Now suppose you branch off to write syrup.md, and meanwhile someone commits a change to pancakes.md on main. The two lines of history have diverged:

Sliding main forward would lose fb4ec2b. Instead, Git makes a new merge commit with two parents, combining both sides. Git opens your editor with a ready-made message, Merge branch 'syrup-page'; close the tab to accept it.

ort is the name of Git's merge algorithm. Look at the shape it made:

Here the two branches changed different files, so Git combined them automatically. When both sides change the same lines, Git stops and asks you to choose; that's a merge conflict, and Module 5 covers it.

#Your repository and GitHub's copy

So far everything has been on your computer. A remote is another copy of the repository that yours knows about, and by convention the main one is called origin. When it lives on GitHub, it looks like this:

Three commands move commits between the copies:

  • git push sends your new commits on a branch up to GitHub.
  • git fetch downloads new commits from GitHub without changing your files.
  • git pull fetches and merges them into your current branch.

Your repository also remembers where GitHub's branches were the last time you talked to it, under names like origin/main. That's how git status can tell you this after you commit without pushing:

#Pull requests: a merge with a conversation

On a team you don't usually merge your own branch into main from the terminal. You push the branch to GitHub and open a pull request (PR): a page that says "please merge add-events-page into main", showing every commit and every changed line. Teammates read it, comment on specific lines, and approve it or ask for changes. Automated checks can run on it too. Only then does someone click Merge pull request.

One detail surprises people: GitHub's default Merge pull request button always makes a merge commit, even when a fast-forward was possible. That keeps a visible record of each PR in the history. The button's menu also offers Squash and merge (combine the PR's commits into one) and Rebase and merge; projects pick whichever they prefer.

#Common mistakes

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting which branch you're on. Before you commit, glance at the first line of git status (On branch …) or the branch name in VS Code's bottom-left corner. Committing to main by mistake is the most common branch error; Practice shows how to move the commit.

⚠️ Watch out

Switching branches with unsaved, uncommitted work. If your edits would be overwritten, Git refuses:

Commit your work (on the right branch), or undo it with git restore, and then switch. Edits that wouldn't clash may come along with you to the other branch, which is confusing in its own way, so make switching with a clean git status a habit.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You're on main and run git switch -c dark-mode, then make two commits. Where does main point?

  • Only the branch you're on moves when you commit. main stayed put.

  • Creating a branch adds a new name; committing then moves only dark-mode.

  • Branches are only deleted when you run git branch -d.

Show answer

B. Creating a branch adds a new name; committing then moves only dark-mode.

2Since you created fix-typo from main, nobody has committed to main. What does git merge fix-typo on main do?

  • main has nothing new, so there's nothing to combine and no merge commit is needed.

  • That happens only when both branches have new commits.

  • Conflicts need both sides to have changed the same lines; here only one side changed.

Show answer

A. main has nothing new, so there's nothing to combine and no merge commit is needed.

3Both main and syrup-page have new commits that touch different files. What does git merge syrup-page produce?

  • Sliding main forward would lose its own new commit, so Git can't fast-forward.

  • That's the Merge made by the 'ort' strategy result, shown as a diamond in git log --graph.

  • Diverged branches are normal; merging them is exactly what git merge is for.

Show answer

B. That's the Merge made by the 'ort' strategy result, shown as a diamond in git log --graph.

4What's the difference between git fetch and git pull?

  • They differ in whether your branch changes.

  • fetch updates names like origin/main but leaves your files alone.

  • Both talk to a remote such as origin.

Show answer

B. fetch updates names like origin/main but leaves your files alone.

Key takeaways

  • A branch is a movable name for a commit; HEAD says which branch you're on. Creating one copies nothing.
  • git switch -c name creates and switches; committing moves only the current branch.
  • A merge fast-forwards when the receiving branch hasn't moved, and makes a two-parent merge commit when both sides have.
  • origin is GitHub's copy; push sends commits up, fetch downloads them, pull downloads and merges.
  • A pull request is a proposed merge with a review and discussion attached; GitHub's default button records it with a merge commit.

#Further reading

  • Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell (opens in a new tab): the classic explanation of branches as pointers, with clear diagrams.
  • Pro Git: Basic Branching and Merging (opens in a new tab): a realistic story of a hotfix and a feature branch, including both kinds of merge.
  • GitHub Docs: GitHub flow (opens in a new tab): GitHub's short description of the branch, pull request, and merge cycle.

The club website from Module 2 lives only on your laptop. In this build you'll put it on GitHub and add an events page the way teams do: on a branch, through a pull request, merged only when it's ready. By the end, git log --graph will show this:

Everything below runs in VS Code's terminal inside ~/git-course/club-site. Your commit IDs will differ.

#Step 1: Create an empty repository on GitHub

  1. On GitHub, click the + in the top-right corner and choose New repository.
  2. Name it club-site. Add a one-line description if you like.
  3. Choose Public or Private. Either works for this course; private is fine if you'd rather keep practice work to yourself.

GitHub shows a Quick Setup page with your repository's address. Pick the SSH address if you set up a key in Module 1, or HTTPS if you're using a credential manager.

#Step 2: Connect your project and push main

Tell your repository about GitHub's copy, naming it origin, then push:

With your username in place of samrivera (or the https://github.com/... address), you'll see something like this. The object counts and speeds vary:

The -u ("upstream") links your main to GitHub's main, so from now on plain git push and git pull know where to go. On Windows with HTTPS, this is when the Git Credential Manager sign-in window appears.

Refresh the GitHub page. Your four files are there, and clicking the commit count shows the same four commits as git log. Notice that drafts/ and .DS_Store aren't: .gitignore kept them home.

#Step 3: Start a branch for the new page

From here until the merge, main doesn't change. If the club needs a quick fix to the home page while you work, someone can make it on another branch without tripping over your half-built page.

#Step 4: Build the page in small commits

Create events.html:

A page nobody can find isn't much use, so link it from the home page. Add this line in index.html below the meetings paragraph, check the diff, and commit:

Read the labels: your branch is two commits ahead, while main and GitHub's origin/main both still point at d873084.

#Step 5: Push the branch

Lines starting with remote: come from GitHub itself, and it's handing you a link to open a pull request. Pushing a branch doesn't change GitHub's main at all.

#Step 6: Open the pull request

Open the repository page on GitHub. A yellow banner says your branch had recent pushes; click Compare & pull request. (The link from the push output goes to the same place.)

  1. Check the branch boxes at the top: base: main ← compare: add-events-page. Read that arrow as "merge add-events-page into main".
  2. Write a title that says what the PR does: Add an events page.
  3. Write a description. Reviewers read it before any code, so answer three questions:
  1. Click Create pull request.

The pull request has tabs worth knowing. Conversation holds the description and every comment. Commits lists your two commits. Files changed shows the combined diff, line by line, and it's where reviewers leave comments.

#Step 7: Review your own pull request, then fix it

Before asking anyone else to look, read your own Files changed tab as if you were the reviewer. Two problems jump out: events.html doesn't load style.css, so it won't match the home page, and there's no way back to the home page. Fix both in events.html on the same branch:

Refresh the pull request: the new commit appears in the conversation and the Files changed diff updates. A pull request follows its branch, so you never need to open a second PR to fix the first one.

#Step 8: Merge on GitHub

Scroll to the bottom of the Conversation tab. GitHub reports whether the branch can merge without conflicts. Click Merge pull request, then Confirm merge. The PR turns purple and is marked Merged.

GitHub then offers a Delete branch button. Click it. The branch's commits are now part of main, so the name is just clutter, and GitHub can restore it if you ever need it.

#Step 9: Bring your computer up to date

The merge happened on GitHub, so your laptop doesn't know about it yet. Switch to main and pull:

That "up to date" line is Git going by the last thing it heard from GitHub, before pulling. Over the network you'll also see a few remote: lines counting objects. The pull fast-forwarded your main to GitHub's merge commit. Now clean up the local branch name and the stale origin/add-events-page label:

Finally, admire the history:

GitHub made a merge commit even though a fast-forward was possible, and named it after the PR. Anyone reading the log later can find PR #1 and its whole discussion.

#The finished events page

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 1, why leave GitHub's "Add a README" option off?

  • It displays them fine; the problem is the extra commit.

  • Your push would then be rejected until you merged the two unrelated histories. An empty repository accepts your existing commits as they are.

  • It already has one, committed in Module 2.

Show answer

B. Your push would then be rejected until you merged the two unrelated histories. An empty repository accepts your existing commits as they are.

2After opening the PR, you found two problems. Why commit and push to the same branch instead of opening a new pull request?

  • The reviewer sees one PR with the whole story, including the fix.

  • Repositories can have any number of open pull requests.

  • That skips review entirely, which is the opposite of the goal.

Show answer

A. The reviewer sees one PR with the whole story, including the fix.

3After merging on GitHub, your local git log still ends at d873084. Why?

  • GitHub marked it Merged; the commits are on GitHub's main.

  • Git only learns about remote changes when you fetch or pull.

  • The merge already exists on GitHub. Pulling brings it down; merging again would be redundant.

Show answer

B. Git only learns about remote changes when you fetch or pull.

Key takeaways

  • git remote add origin <url> plus git push -u origin main puts an existing project on GitHub.
  • Build features on a branch and push the branch; GitHub's main stays untouched until the merge.
  • A good PR description says what changed, why, and how to check it.
  • New commits pushed to a PR's branch update the PR, so fixes go on the same branch.
  • After merging on GitHub: switch to main, git pull, delete the local branch, and git fetch --prune.

Work in ~/git-course/practice, making a fresh repository for each exercise unless it says otherwise. Keep git log --oneline --graph --all handy: it's the fastest way to see what your branches are doing.

#Warm-up: read the labels

Which branch are you on? How many branches have work that main doesn't? If you ran git merge add-timer right now, would it fast-forward?

Show solution

You're on main (that's where HEAD -> points). Two branches, add-scoreboard and add-timer, each have one commit that main doesn't. Merging add-timer would fast-forward, because main hasn't moved since either branch started.

#Exercise 1: Fast-forward or merge commit?

For each picture, you're on main and about to run git merge feature. Predict the result before opening the solution.

Need a hint?

Ask one question: does main have any commits that feature doesn't? If not, Git can just slide main forward.

Show solution
  • A: fast-forward. main hasn't moved since feature started, so main slides forward to F2. No new commit.
  • B: merge commit. Both sides have a new commit (B2 and F1). Git creates a commit with two parents.
  • C: nothing to do. feature was already merged, and main has moved on. Git prints Already up to date. because every commit on feature is already in main.

On GitHub, the default Merge pull request button would make a merge commit in A too, because GitHub always records the PR.

#Exercise 2: Two features at the same time

In a new quiz-app repository with one commit, create two branches from main: add-timer (commit a timer.txt) and add-scoreboard (commit a scores.txt). Make sure each branch starts from main, not from the other branch. Then merge both into main and delete them.

Before merging, predict: which merge will fast-forward, and which will make a merge commit?

Need a hint?

Run git switch main before creating the second branch, or it will start from add-timer. After the first merge, has main moved?

Show solution

The first merge fast-forwards. But now main has a commit (6fbef63) that add-scoreboard doesn't, so the second one can't:

Finish with git branch -d add-timer add-scoreboard. This is exactly what happens on a team when two pull requests are open at once: whichever merges second needs a merge commit.

#Exercise 3: You committed to main by mistake

In a repository connected to a remote, you meant to start a branch but forgot, and committed straight to main. git status gives it away:

Move that commit onto a new branch called add-space-round, and put main back where origin/main is. You haven't pushed. Don't lose the commit.

Need a hint?

Two steps. First, stick a new branch name on the commit you're on, so it's saved. Then move main back one commit with git reset --keep HEAD~1 (HEAD~1 means "the commit before this one").

Show solution

git branch add-space-round creates a name pointing at your commit, so the commit is safe. git reset --keep HEAD~1 then moves main back one commit. --keep refuses to run if it would destroy uncommitted changes, which makes it a safer choice than --hard for this job.

Only do this before pushing. If the commit is already on GitHub's main, rewriting main would break everyone else's copy.

#Exercise 4: Delete branches without losing work

Your quiz-app repository has three branches:

fix-typo was merged into main. experiment was a rainbow theme you decided against and never merged. Use Git to check which branches are merged, delete both, and explain why Git treats them differently.

Need a hint?

git branch --merged and git branch --no-merged list branches by whether main already contains their commits. Try -d on both before reaching for anything stronger.

Show solution

-d is the safe delete: it only removes a branch whose commits are already in main, because only the name is lost. Deleting experiment would orphan its commit, so Git asks you to be sure. Since you really don't want the rainbow theme, force it:

Make -d your habit and use -D only after reading that warning.

#Exercise 5: Write a PR description a reviewer can use

A teammate's branch makes this change to the club website's style.css. Write the pull request title and description.

Context: two club members said the site was hard to read on their phones.

Need a hint?

Cover what changed, why, and how a reviewer can check it in under a minute. Skip "I changed style.css"; the diff already shows that.

Show solution

One good version:

The title works on its own in a list of PRs. The "how to check it" section saves the reviewer from guessing what to test.

#Exercise 6: Bring main's new work into your branch

You're halfway through add-hints when a teammate's PR changing timer.txt gets merged into main. You want to test your hints with the new timer before opening your PR. Starting from this situation, update your branch:

Need a hint?

Merging works in either direction. Switch to the branch that should receive the commits, then merge the other one in.

Show solution

Your branch now has everything from main plus your hint. On a real team, run git switch main and git pull first so your main matches GitHub. If both sides had edited the same lines, this is where a conflict would appear, and it's better to meet it on your branch than in the middle of someone's review.

#Challenge: Recreate this history exactly

Make a new maze-game repository whose git log --oneline --graph has this shape, with these messages:

One catch: the hotfix merge must be a fast-forward, so your final graph shows no second merge commit. Delete both branches at the end.

Need a hint?

Work in the order the commits appear. You need main to receive a commit while levels exists, then merge levels. Create hotfix after that merge, and don't commit to main before merging hotfix.

Show solution

The diagram draws the hotfix merge as a dot, but Git fast-forwarded it, so Fix crash on start sits directly on top of the merge commit. That's the gap between a picture of intent and what Git actually records.

What you'll learn

  • Write an issue with a clear problem, steps to reproduce, and acceptance criteria.
  • Sort work with labels and assignees, and track it on a GitHub project board.
  • Link a pull request to an issue so merging closes it automatically.
  • Review a pull request with line comments and suggested changes, and choose between Comment, Approve, and Request changes.

Issue #7 on the club website said, in full: "Fix the signup page." Jordan picked it up and opened a pull request that made the signup button bigger and brighter. Alex glanced at it, typed "LGTM" (looks good to me), and approved it forty seconds later. It merged.

The next morning the real problem was still there: the form rejected any email address with a + in it, like sam+club@example.com, so two new members couldn't sign up. Nobody did anything lazy on purpose. The issue never said what was wrong, and the review never checked whether the change solved it. This lesson is about the two cheap habits that would have caught it: writing the problem down properly, and reviewing against it.

#An issue is a written-down problem anyone can pick up

An issue is a numbered page in a GitHub repository for one bug, idea, or task. It has a title, a description written in Markdown, a comment thread, and a sidebar for labels, assignees, and links. Because it's numbered, you can refer to it anywhere on GitHub as #7, and GitHub turns that into a link.

A good issue lets someone who wasn't in the room start work without asking you anything. Here's issue #7 rewritten:

The parts that matter most:

  • A title that states the problem, not the fix. "Signup form rejects emails that contain a plus sign" beats "Fix signup".
  • Steps to reproduce, so anyone can see the bug for themselves. If they can't make it happen, they can't prove it's fixed.
  • Expected versus actual, which turns "it's broken" into something checkable.
  • Acceptance criteria ("Done when"): a checklist that both the author and the reviewer will use. GitHub renders - [ ] as clickable checkboxes.

Feature requests follow the same shape: what problem the user has, what they'd like to happen, and what "done" looks like.

#Labels and assignees sort the pile

A busy repository has dozens of open issues. Labels are colored tags for sorting them. Every new repository starts with a standard set, including:

Label Use it for
bug Something is broken or behaving unexpectedly
enhancement A new feature or improvement
documentation README and docs changes
good first issue Small, well-described tasks for newcomers
help wanted The maintainers would welcome outside help
question Needs more information before anyone can act
duplicate, invalid, wontfix Reasons an issue is being closed without a change

You can rename these or add your own from the Labels page in Issues. An assignee is the person doing the work; assigning yourself is how you say "I've got this" so two people don't fix the same bug.

#A project board shows who's doing what

A list of issues tells you what exists. A project board tells you where each piece of work stands. GitHub Projects lets you create a board, add issues and pull requests to it as cards, and drag them between columns. A new board starts with a Status field whose columns are Todo, In Progress, and Done, plus a No Status column for anything not yet sorted. Many teams add an In review column.

Boards also automate the boring part. Two built-in workflows are on by default: when an issue or pull request on the board is closed, or a pull request is merged, its card moves to Done.

#Link the pull request so the issue closes itself

Write a closing keyword followed by the issue number in your pull request's description:

GitHub links the two pages, shows the PR in the issue's sidebar, and closes the issue the moment the PR is merged. The keywords are close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves, and resolved, in any capitalization. Two details trip people up:

  • It only works when the pull request merges into the repository's default branch (usually main).
  • Words like "Related to #7" or "See #7" create a link but don't close anything. That's useful when a PR is only part of the fix.

#Code review: read the change against the issue

A review is a teammate reading your pull request before it merges. On the Files changed tab, a reviewer can hover over any line and click the blue comment icon to comment on it. They can comment once, or click Start a review to collect several comments as pending (visible only to them) and send them together, which gives the author one notification instead of ten.

When they finish, they submit the review as one of three types:

Review type Means Use it when
Comment Feedback, no verdict You have questions, or you only looked at part of it
Approve Ready to merge It meets the acceptance criteria and you'd be comfortable shipping it
Request changes Must be fixed first Something is wrong or missing

GitHub won't let you approve your own pull request; only someone else can do that.

What should a reviewer actually check? In order of importance:

  1. Does it solve the issue? Walk through the "Done when" list. This is the step Alex skipped.
  2. Does it work? For small projects, check out the branch and try it. For the signup bug: does sam+club@example.com go through now?
  3. Did it break anything else? Does a bad address still get rejected?
  4. Can the next person understand it? Clear names, no leftover test code, no secrets.

#Suggested changes

For small fixes, typing "there's a typo on line 12" makes the author find and fix it by hand. A suggested change does it in one click. In a line comment, the reviewer clicks the suggestion button in the comment toolbar, which inserts a block containing the current line, and edits it:

The author sees the old and new lines side by side with a Commit suggestion button. Clicking it adds a commit to the PR's branch, crediting the reviewer as co-author. With several suggestions, Add suggestion to batch combines them into one commit.

#Review etiquette that keeps teams friendly

Reviews go wrong more often from tone than from code. Compare:

Unhelpful Helpful
"This is wrong." "This rejects a+b@example.com, which issue #7 says should work. Could the pattern allow +?"
"Why would you do it this way?" "I'd have reached for a <label> here. Was there a reason for the <span>?"
"LGTM" (after reading nothing) "Tested both addresses from the issue; both behave as described. Approving."
A comment on every tiny thing, all blocking "nit: extra blank line. Not blocking."

As a reviewer: comment on the code, never the person. Explain why, so the author learns something. Ask questions when you're unsure instead of declaring. Mark small preferences as nit: so the author knows they're optional, and say what you liked. Review promptly; a PR waiting three days goes stale.

As an author: keep pull requests small so they can be reviewed properly. Reply to every comment, even with "Done in 3f2a1c9". Click Resolve conversation once you've handled a comment. If you disagree, say why calmly; the reviewer might be missing context, or you might be. Then re-request a review so they know it's their turn.

#Common mistakes

⚠️ Watch out

Rubber-stamp approvals. An approval says "I checked this and it's ready." If you only skimmed, submit a Comment saying what you did and didn't check. The signup bug shipped because an approval meant less than it looked.

⚠️ Watch out

Applying a suggestion on GitHub, then pushing from your laptop. Commit suggestion adds a commit to the branch on GitHub. Your local branch doesn't have it, so your next git push gets rejected. Run git pull on the branch first, then keep working.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Which issue title gives a developer the most to work with?

  • It says something's wrong but not what, so the first reply will be a question.

  • That names a solution, which might be the wrong one. Describe the problem and let the fix follow.

  • It names the page, the input that fails, and the behavior, so anyone can reproduce it.

Show answer

C. It names the page, the input that fails, and the behavior, so anyone can reproduce it.

2Your PR description says "Related to #7". You merge it into main. What happens to issue #7?

  • Only closing keywords such as Closes, Fixes, or Resolves close an issue on merge.

  • "Related to" just references the issue, which is right when the PR is only part of the fix.

  • Mentioning an issue number is always allowed; it just creates a link.

Show answer

B. "Related to" just references the issue, which is right when the PR is only part of the fix.

3Reviewing a PR, you find that the new contact link points to a misspelled email address, so messages would bounce. Which review type fits?

  • Approving tells everyone it's ready to merge, but this would ship a broken link.

  • It's a real defect, so it should block the merge, and a suggestion makes the fix one click.

  • "nit" signals something optional. A link that doesn't work isn't optional.

Show answer

B. It's a real defect, so it should block the merge, and a suggestion makes the fix one click.

4A reviewer writes "nit: I'd put the footer styles at the end of the file." What are they telling you?

  • "nit" (short for nitpick) marks small, non-blocking comments.

  • That would be a blocking comment, usually sent with Request changes.

  • A bug would be described as a problem, not a preference.

Show answer

A. "nit" (short for nitpick) marks small, non-blocking comments.

Key takeaways

  • A good issue has a problem-stating title, steps to reproduce, expected versus actual behavior, and a "Done when" checklist.
  • Labels sort issues, assignees claim them, and a project board shows each one's status.
  • Closes #7 in a PR description closes the issue when the PR merges into the default branch.
  • Review against the issue first: does it solve the problem, does it work, did it break anything?
  • Use suggested changes for small fixes, mark optional comments as nit:, and always explain why.

#Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Linking a pull request to an issue (opens in a new tab): every closing keyword and the default-branch rule.
  • Google Engineering Practices: How to do a code review (opens in a new tab): Google's public guide for reviewers, short and practical.
  • GitHub Docs: Quickstart for Projects (opens in a new tab): set up a board with views, fields, and automations.
