What you'll learn

  • Write an issue with acceptance criteria, label it, assign it, and track it on a project board.
  • Name a branch after its issue and link the pull request with Closes #2.
  • Review a partner's pull request with a suggested change and a Request changes review.
  • Respond to feedback: apply a suggestion, pull it locally, push a fix, resolve conversations, and merge.

Last module, you merged a pull request that only you had read. Real projects add two things around that: a written plan before the work starts, and a second person checking the work against the plan. In this build you'll run one complete cycle on club-site with a partner, where one of you is the author and the other reviews. Then swap roles and do it again on the other person's repository.

The examples use Sam as the author and Priya as the reviewer.

#Step 1: Invite your partner

Your partner needs access to your repository before GitHub will let you request their review. On your club-site repository, open Settings, click Collaborators in the Access section, then Add people, and search for your partner's username. They accept the invitation from their email or notifications.

📝 Note

Working alone? Do every step yourself except approving. GitHub doesn't allow authors to approve their own pull requests, but you can still leave line comments on your own PR and submit them as a Comment review. Reading your own diff as a stranger would is a skill worth practicing anyway.

#Step 2: Write the issue

New members have no way to reach the club between meetings. On GitHub, open Issues, click New issue, and write:

Before submitting, use the sidebar: click Labels and pick enhancement and good first issue, then click Assignees and assign yourself. Click Submit new issue. GitHub numbers it #2, because pull request #1 already used the first number; issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence.

The "Done when" list is the most important part. In Step 6 your reviewer will check the work against it, item by item.

#Step 3: Track it on a project board

  1. Click your profile picture, then Your profile, then the Projects tab, and New project.
  2. Under Start from scratch, choose Board, name it Club website, and click Create project.
  3. Back on issue #2, click Projects in the sidebar and choose Club website.

The issue appears as a card. When you start working, drag it to In Progress so your partner can see it's claimed. You won't need to move it to Done: the board's built-in workflow does that when the pull request merges.

#Step 4: Branch, build, commit

Always start from an up-to-date main:

Starting the branch name with the issue number is a common convention; anyone listing branches can find the issue behind each one. (The issue's sidebar also has a Create a branch link under Development that does this for you on GitHub.)

Add the contact line to index.html under the events link. This version has a typo in it on purpose; leave it in so your reviewer has something real to catch:

The push output looks like Module 3's, ending with GitHub's link to open a pull request.

#Step 5: Open the pull request and ask for a review

Click Compare & pull request. Title it Add the club's contact email, and in the description, link the issue:

Click Create pull request. It becomes #3. In the sidebar, click Reviewers and choose your partner. Check the issue page: under Development, it now lists PR #3.

Notice that this PR doesn't do everything the issue asked for yet. That's realistic, and it's exactly what review is for.

#Step 6: Review your partner's pull request

Switch roles. As the reviewer, open the PR from your notifications or the repository's Pull requests tab. Read the description and the linked issue first, so you know what "done" means. Then open Files changed.

A suggested change for the typo. Hover over the new line in index.html and click the blue comment icon. Click the suggestion button in the comment toolbar; it inserts the current line inside a suggestion block. Fix both misspellings in that block and add a sentence explaining why:

Click Start a review. The comment is now pending, visible only to you.

A comment about the missing requirement. The issue's second checkbox says the events page should show the email, and events.html isn't in this PR at all. That can't be a line comment on a file that didn't change, so save it for the summary.

Submit. Click Review changes (in GitHub's newer layout the button reads Submit review), write a summary, choose Request changes, and submit:

The summary says exactly what's blocking, points back to the issue, and mentions what worked.

#Step 7: Respond to the review

Switch back to the author. Open the PR and find the suggestion. Click Commit suggestion, replace GitHub's generic message with Fix spelling of the club email, and confirm. GitHub adds that commit to your branch and credits your partner as co-author.

That commit exists only on GitHub. Pull it before doing anything else on your laptop:

The commit message carries the credit as a trailer, a line GitHub reads to show both people's pictures on the commit:

Now handle the second point. Add the same line to events.html, above the "Back to home" link:

⚠️ Watch out

If you skip the git pull and push anyway, Git refuses with a [rejected] message and a hint to pull first, because GitHub's branch has a commit yours doesn't. That's Git protecting the reviewer's suggestion, not an error in your work. Run git pull, then push again.

On the PR's Conversation tab, reply to the review: "Fixed the typo with your suggestion, and added the email to events.html in 8e79849." Click Resolve conversation on the suggestion thread. Then, next to your partner's name under Reviewers, click the re-request icon so they know it's their turn.

#Step 8: Approve, merge, and watch the issue close

As the reviewer, walk through the "Done when" list once more: home page link, events page link, spelling. All three pass, so submit a review with Approve and a short note on what you checked.

As the author, click Merge pull request, Confirm merge, and Delete branch. Now look around:

  • Issue #2 shows Closed, with a note that PR #3 closed it.
  • On the Club website board, the card has moved to Done by itself.

#Step 9: Sync your laptop

Three commits tell the honest story: the first attempt, the reviewer's fix, and the missing requirement. Now swap roles and repeat the cycle on your partner's repository.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did the reviewer leave the "missing events page" point in the review summary rather than as a line comment?

  • They can; #2 links from any comment.

  • Line comments attach to lines in Files changed. Feedback about something missing belongs in the summary.

  • A review can hold any number of line comments.

Show answer

B. Line comments attach to lines in Files changed. Feedback about something missing belongs in the summary.

2After clicking Commit suggestion on GitHub, why must the author run git pull before pushing again?

  • Pushing without it would be rejected; pulling first fast-forwards the local branch.

  • The commit lands on the PR's own branch.

  • The issue closes when the PR merges; pulling only updates your laptop.

Show answer

A. Pushing without it would be rejected; pulling first fast-forwards the local branch.

3The PR description says Closes #2, but suppose the PR had targeted a branch called dev instead of main. What happens when it merges?

  • Closing keywords only act when a PR merges into the repository's default branch.

  • You'd close it by hand, or when dev is later merged into main by a PR that says Closes #2.

  • The merge works fine; only the automatic closing is skipped.

Show answer

B. You'd close it by hand, or when dev is later merged into main by a PR that says Closes #2.

Key takeaways

  • Put acceptance criteria in the issue; the reviewer checks against them, which catches requirements the author missed.
  • Name branches after issues and put Closes #N in the PR description so merging closes the issue and updates the board.
  • Batch comments with Start a review, use suggested changes for small fixes, and put "something's missing" points in the summary.
  • After committing a suggestion on GitHub, git pull before you push.
  • Reply to every comment, resolve handled conversations, and re-request review when it's the reviewer's turn.

#Extend it

  • Add a pull request template so every PR starts with the right headings: create .github/pull_request_template.md containing Closes #, ## What, and ## How to check it, and merge it through a PR. Open another PR and watch the description fill itself in.
  • Add an issue template at .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/feature.md with front matter (name, about, labels) and a body containing the three headings from Step 2.
  • Add an In review column to the board, and move cards there when a PR is opened.

#Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Reviewing proposed changes in a pull request (opens in a new tab): line comments, pending reviews, and the three review types.
  • GitHub Docs: Incorporating feedback in your pull request (opens in a new tab): committing and batching suggestions, and re-requesting review.
  • GitHub Docs: Using the built-in automations (opens in a new tab): the board workflows that moved your card to Done.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn vague requests into issues with steps to reproduce and a "Done when" list.
  • Split oversized tasks into issues that each fit in one pull request.
  • Predict which pull request descriptions will close an issue on merge.
  • Review a diff against its issue, write kind and specific comments, and reply to feedback as an author.

Most of these exercises are writing, not commands, because that's what planning and review mostly are. Write your answers in a scratch file, or better, try them for real in your club-site repository's issues and pull requests. Compare with the solutions afterward; many good answers are possible.

#Warm-up: pick the labels

Using GitHub's default labels, label each issue. Some need two.

  1. "The 'Back to home' link on events.html goes to a 404 page."
  2. "Could we add a photo gallery of past robots?"
  3. "README doesn't say how to preview the site."
  4. "Is the club open to 6th graders?"
Show solution
  1. bug: something that should work doesn't.
  2. enhancement: a new feature. If it's simple and well described, add good first issue too.
  3. documentation, and probably good first issue, since it's a small, low-risk change.
  4. question. It isn't a code change at all, so it might be answered and closed, or moved to wherever the club handles questions.

#Exercise 1: Rewrite a vague bug report

A club member files this:

Rewrite it as an issue a teammate could fix without asking any questions. You discover by testing that on a 375px-wide screen, the longest event line runs off the right edge and the page scrolls sideways.

Need a hint?

Use the four parts from the Notes: a title that states the problem, steps to reproduce, expected versus actual, and a "Done when" checklist. Include the screen width, since that's what makes it reproducible.

Show solution

The title now says where and what. Anyone can see the bug in under a minute, and the reviewer knows exactly what to check.

#Exercise 2: Split an issue that's too big

The club president opens one issue: "Redesign the website." It has twelve bullet points, from a new color scheme to a members-only login. Explain why one issue is a problem here, and split it into four smaller issues with good titles, choosing the parts you'd do first.

Need a hint?

Think about the pull request that would close the big issue. How long would a review of it take? What happens if one part is controversial and the rest isn't?

Show solution

One giant issue becomes one giant pull request: hard to review properly, impossible to merge piece by piece, and blocked entirely if one part (say, the login) needs a long discussion. Smaller issues can be assigned to different people and finished in parallel.

A good split, each about one PR:

  • Pick a club color palette and apply it in style.css
  • Add a shared navigation bar to the home and events pages
  • Make all pages readable on 375px-wide screens
  • Add a photo gallery page

The login idea becomes a question issue first ("Do we need members-only pages?"), because it needs a decision before anyone writes code. You can keep the original issue open as a checklist that links to the small ones, then close it when they're done.

#Exercise 3: Will it close the issue?

Issue #12 is open. The repository's default branch is main. For each merged pull request below, does #12 close automatically?

PR Targets Description contains
A main Fixes #12
B main RESOLVES: #12
C main Related to #12
D dev Closes #12
E main Closes #11, #12
Need a hint?

Two rules from the Notes: the keyword must come right before each issue number, and the PR must merge into the default branch. Keywords can be any capitalization and can have a colon.

Show solution
  • A: closes. A keyword, then the issue, into main.
  • B: closes. Capital letters and a colon are both allowed.
  • C: doesn't close. "Related to" creates a link but isn't a closing keyword. Right for a PR that's only part of the work.
  • D: doesn't close. Keywords are ignored when a PR targets a branch other than the default.
  • E: closes #11 only. Each issue needs its own keyword: Closes #11, closes #12.

#Exercise 4: Rewrite harsh review comments

Rewrite each comment so it's specific, explains why, and treats the author as a teammate. Keep the technical point.

The context: (1) the new "Join" link points to join.htm but the file is join.html; (2) the PR adds style="color: blue" to five paragraphs; (3) the events are written as separate <p> tags.

Need a hint?

A useful shape is: what you noticed, why it matters, and what you'd suggest (as a question if you're unsure). Mark optional preferences as nit:.

Show solution
  1. "The Join link points to join.htm, but the file is join.html, so it 404s for me. Suggestion attached." Then attach a suggested change with the fixed line. This is blocking.
  2. "These five paragraphs each set style="color: blue". Could we move that into one rule in style.css? Then changing the color later is a one-line edit." Probably not blocking, but worth fixing in this PR.
  3. "nit: a <ul> might be a nice fit for the events, since screen readers announce how many items a list has. Fine to leave as-is if you'd rather." Optional, and it says so.

All three keep the point and lose the sting. Notice that none of them uses "you" as the subject of a criticism; they describe the code.

#Exercise 5: Review a pull request against its issue

Here's issue #9 and the pull request meant to close it. Find every problem, decide which ones block merging, and write the review: a summary, the review type, and at least one suggested change.

Need a hint?

Walk the "Done when" list line by line, then read every changed line. Which file isn't in the diff at all? And is colour a CSS property? (Browsers quietly ignore properties they don't recognize.)

Show solution

Three findings:

  1. Blocking: the events page isn't updated. events.html doesn't appear in the diff, so the second checkbox fails.
  2. Blocking: colour isn't a CSS property. CSS uses the American spelling, color. The browser silently ignores the rule, so the footer won't be gray and the third checkbox fails.
  3. Not blocking: an extra blank line at the end of style.css.

Line comment on colour: gray;:

Review summary, submitted as Request changes:

The first problem is the kind a quick skim misses, because nothing in the diff looks wrong. You only catch it by checking the issue.

#Exercise 6: Answer a review as the author

You opened a PR adding a gallery page. Your reviewer left three comments. Write a reply to each.

You agree with A. You'd rather keep the name in B because the issue calls it "gallery". For C, you know Drive links for that folder require a sign-in, so visitors couldn't see the images.

Need a hint?

Every comment deserves a reply, even when you don't change anything. When you disagree, give the reason so the reviewer can weigh it. Point to the commit when you've made a fix.

Show solution
  • A: "Good catch, thanks. Added alt text for all three robots in 4d1e0b2." Then click Resolve conversation.
  • B: "I'd like to keep gallery.html to match the wording in issue #14 and the nav link. Happy to rename if you feel strongly." A nit is optional, so declining politely is fine.
  • C: "I looked into that, but the Drive folder needs a sign-in, so visitors would see broken images. The three photos are under 200 KB each, so committing them seemed safer. Does that work for you?" A respectful disagreement with a reason and a question back.

Then re-request review so the reviewer knows it's their turn.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why Git merges some edits by itself and stops on others.
  • Read <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers and say which side is which.
  • Resolve a conflict, check for leftover markers, and finish the merge.
  • Choose between merging and rebasing, and park unfinished work with git stash.
  • Pick the right place to record a decision: README, CHANGELOG, or a decision record.

Maya and Leo improve the same quiz game on the same afternoon. On her branch, Maya adds a music category. On main, Leo adds sports. Both edits land on the same lines of settings.json, so when you merge Maya's branch, Git prints this and stops:

Nothing is broken and nothing is lost: both versions are safe in commits. Git is asking a question it can't answer for you. What should these lines say now?

#Git compares three versions, not two

Picture two friends who each get a photocopy of the same essay. If one fixes paragraph 1 and the other fixes paragraph 4, anyone could combine the copies. If both rewrite paragraph 2, a person has to read both and decide.

Git works the same way. When you run git merge, it finds the merge base, the newest commit both branches share. Then it walks through each file and asks who changed each region since the base:

  • Nobody changed it: keep it.
  • Only one branch changed it: take that branch's version.
  • Both changed the same lines, or lines right next to each other: stop and ask a human.

The "right next to each other" part surprises people, because Git compares lines, not JSON keys. When I changed the title on one branch and the time limit on the very next line on another, Git reported a conflict. Changing the time limit and the theme, two lines apart, merged on its own:

#Reading the conflict markers

After a failed merge, git status lists the files that need you:

"Both modified" means both branches changed this file in overlapping places. Open it and Git has written both versions into the file, fenced off with markers:

Read it from top to bottom:

  • <<<<<<< HEAD starts the version from your current branch, the one you were on when you typed git merge (here main). VS Code labels this the Current Change.
  • ======= separates the two versions.
  • >>>>>>> add-music ends the version from the branch coming in. VS Code calls it the Incoming Change.
  • Everything outside the markers merged cleanly. Leave it alone.

Notice "history", above the markers. Both branches added the same comma there, so Git counted it as agreed.

💡 Tip

To also see what the lines said at the merge base, merge with the zdiff3 style: git -c merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3 merge add-music. A middle section starting with ||||||| shows the original lines, which makes it easier to see what each person meant.

#Resolving means deciding what the file should say

Resolving is three steps: edit the file until it is right, mark it resolved with git add, then commit.

Here both new categories belong in the game, so delete the three marker lines and keep both entries. That looks finished, but "sports" now needs a comma because another item follows it. Keeping both sides by deleting markers often breaks the syntax, so check the result. If you have Python installed, it can test a JSON file (type python instead of python3 on Windows):

Add the comma after "sports" and the same command prints the file back with no error. Then finish the merge:

git diff --check printed nothing, which is what you want. Had a marker survived, it would print lines like settings.json:7: leftover conflict marker. The merge commit at the top has two parents, so the graph shows two lines joining.

Changed your mind halfway through? git merge --abort puts every file back exactly as it was before you typed git merge.

#The same fix in VS Code

VS Code colors each conflict and puts four links above it: Accept Current Change, Accept Incoming Change, Accept Both Changes, and Compare Changes. For more room, click Resolve in Merge Editor, which shows the incoming version, the current version, and an editable Result. Complete Merge stages the file. The next lesson walks through it click by click.

The buttons pick text. They don't check meaning: Accept Both Changes on this file gives the same missing comma.

#Merge or rebase: two ways to catch up with main

Your branch has fallen behind main, and there are two ways to catch up.

  • git merge main, run on your branch, adds a merge commit that ties the histories together. Nothing that exists changes.
  • git rebase main lifts your commits off and replays them on top of the newest main, as if you had started today. History becomes one straight line.

Here is a real rebase of a branch with two commits:

Compare the IDs: 5d4c230 became 0e01462. Rebase makes new commits with the same changes. That's harmless for commits only you have, but a teammate who already pulled the old ones now has a history that disagrees with yours. So rebase only commits you haven't shared, and merge when in doubt. Conflicts can stop a rebase too; you fix them the same way and run git rebase --continue.

#Stash: a pocket for half-finished work

You're halfway through an edit when a teammate needs a quick fix on main, and Git refuses to switch branches:

git stash saves your uncommitted changes and gives you a clean folder. git stash pop brings them back and removes them from the stash.

Switch, fix, switch back, and run git stash pop. New files Git doesn't track yet stay behind unless you add -u. A stash is for minutes or hours; for anything longer, commit to a branch.

#Write down what you decided, and why

A merge commit records what the file says now, not why. Three documents serve three readers:

  • README.md, for newcomers: what the project is, how to run it, what each setting does. Update it in the same pull request that changes the behavior.
  • CHANGELOG.md, for users: notable changes per version under headings like Added, Changed, and Fixed, with an Unreleased section on top.
  • A decision record, for future teammates: one short numbered file per significant choice, often in docs/decisions/. When a later choice replaces it, write a new record and mark the old one superseded.

⚠️ Watch out

Three classic conflict mistakes.

  1. Committing with markers still in the file. Git won't stop you. Run git diff --check before git add.
  2. Clicking Accept Current Change just to make the conflict go away. That silently throws out a teammate's work. If you can't tell what their change was for, ask them.
  3. Rebasing a branch other people use. Their copies keep the old commits and the next pull mixes old with new. Merge instead.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Branch A changes line 2 of settings.json. Branch B changes line 9 and nothing else. What happens when you merge B into A?

  • Only one branch touched each region, so Git takes each change from the side that made it.

  • Conflicts are about overlapping or adjacent lines, not whole files.

  • Git never drops a change just because it came from the incoming branch.

Show answer

A. Only one branch touched each region, so Git takes each change from the side that made it.

2You are on main and run git merge add-music. Which version sits between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======?

  • HEAD is the branch you are on when you start the merge, so its lines come first.

  • The incoming branch's lines come after ======= and end at >>>>>>> add-music.

  • The base only appears in a ||||||| section, and only with the diff3 or zdiff3 style turned on.

Show answer

A. HEAD is the branch you are on when you start the merge, so its lines come first.

3After resolving, git diff --check prints settings.json:7: leftover conflict marker. What should you do next?

  • That would commit a broken file with a marker in it.

  • The check is telling you exactly which line still has a marker. Fix it before staging.

  • Aborting works, but it throws away the resolving you already did for one stray line.

Show answer

B. The check is telling you exactly which line still has a marker. Fix it before staging.

4You pushed your branch team-size yesterday and a classmate added a commit on top of it. Now main has moved ahead. What is the safest way to catch up?

  • Rebase rewrites commits your classmate already has, and your histories split.

  • Merging adds one new commit and leaves every shared commit exactly as it was.

  • Stash parks uncommitted edits. It doesn't bring a branch up to date.

Show answer

B. Merging adds one new commit and leaves every shared commit exactly as it was.

Key takeaways

  • Git compares both branches with their merge base and stops only when both changed the same or neighboring lines.
  • <<<<<<< HEAD to ======= is your current branch; ======= to >>>>>>> is the incoming one.
  • Resolve, run git diff --check, then git add and git commit. git merge --abort is always a way out.
  • Rebase replays your commits as new ones, so use it only on commits you haven't shared.
  • git stash parks uncommitted work briefly; -u includes new files.
  • README explains the project, CHANGELOG lists changes per version, a decision record explains why.

#Further reading

  • Pro Git: Basic Branching and Merging (opens in a new tab): the "Basic Merge Conflicts" section shows another full conflict from start to finish.
  • VS Code: Merge conflicts (opens in a new tab): the official guide to the inline actions and the merge editor, with screenshots.
  • Pro Git: Rebasing (opens in a new tab): read "The Perils of Rebasing" for the longer version of the shared-branch rule.

What you'll learn

  • Create a merge conflict on purpose and recognize it from Git's output.
  • Resolve it in VS Code's merge editor by writing a result neither side had.
  • Finish the merge and clean up the merged branch.
  • Record the decision in a decision record, the README, and a CHANGELOG.

Here is the history you'll have at the end of this lesson. Two teammates changed the same game setting in opposite directions, and the merge commit keeps both of their goals:

Along with it come four files: settings.json, a README that explains every setting, a CHANGELOG, and docs/decisions/0001-hard-mode-gets-its-own-settings.md. Your commit IDs will be different from these; everything else should match.

#Step 1: Make the practice repo

Open VS Code, then open its terminal with Terminal › New Terminal. Make a folder and turn it into a repository:

Use File › Open Folder… to open quiz-night in VS Code, and create two files in it.

Commit both:

#Step 2: Play two teammates

You'll play both people. Maya wants a hard mode: less time and more questions. On a new branch, change time_limit_seconds to 15 and questions_per_round to 20, then commit:

Leo noticed that slower readers run out of time. Back on main, change time_limit_seconds from 30 to 60 and commit:

On a real team, Leo's commit would reach main through a merged pull request and you'd get it with git pull. The conflict that follows is identical either way.

#Step 3: Merge and meet the conflict

Still on main, merge Maya's branch:

Predict before you look: which lines will be inside the markers? Both branches edited line 3, and Maya also edited line 4, right next to it. Git treats touching changes as one block, so both lines end up in the conflict:

#Step 4: Resolve it in the merge editor

Open the Source Control view (Ctrl+Shift+G, or ⌃⇧G on a Mac). settings.json is listed under Merge Changes. Click it to open the file, then click the Resolve in Merge Editor button in the editor.

The merge editor has three parts:

  • Incoming (top left): Maya's version from hard-mode.
  • Current (top right): Leo's version, already on main.
  • Result (bottom): what the file will say when you finish. You can type in it.

Each side has its own controls to accept it into the Result. Before you click anything, ask what each one would do:

Choice What the game does Who loses
Accept Current Every round is 60 s, 10 questions Maya: hard mode is gone
Accept Incoming Every round is 15 s, 20 questions Leo: slow readers time out again
Accept both Two time_limit_seconds keys in one object Everyone: most JSON readers silently keep the last one, 15

None of them keeps both goals, because one number can't be 60 and 15 at once. The fix is a change in shape: keep Leo's values as the default and give hard mode its own block. Type this into the Result pane so the whole file reads:

Check the commas: every line inside an object ends with one except the last. Then click Complete Merge. VS Code saves the file and stages it, which is the same as running git add settings.json.

💡 Tip

Stuck halfway? Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or ⇧⌘P on a Mac) and run Git: Abort Merge, or type git merge --abort in the terminal. Both put the files back as they were before Step 3.

#Step 5: Commit the merge

Back in the terminal, confirm Git agrees the conflict is settled:

Commit with a message that says how you resolved it, so the history explains itself:

git branch -d only deletes a branch whose work is already merged, so it's safe here. Maya's commit 0e2db9c is still in history; only the label went away.

#Step 6: Write the decision record

In six months someone will open settings.json, see two time limits, and wonder why. Make a folder docs/decisions and add this file:

Context, Decision, and Consequences are the three parts of the classic format. Consequences is the part people skip, and it's the most useful: here it tells the next programmer about work that still needs doing.

#Step 7: Update the README and start a CHANGELOG

Replace the Settings section of README.md so a newcomer can understand every setting without opening the JSON:

Then create CHANGELOG.md. Nothing has been released yet, so both changes go under Unreleased:

Commit the three documents together, since they describe one decision:

#The finished repo

Keep this folder. The next module adds a license and turns it into version 1.0.0, and the one after that adds automatic tests.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why didn't any of the merge editor's accept buttons give the right answer in Step 4?

  • It handles any text file. The problem was the content, not the file type.

  • Resolving well meant changing the file's shape, which only you could decide.

  • The theme line was outside the conflict, so every choice kept it.

Show answer

B. Resolving well meant changing the file's shape, which only you could decide.

2Why does the merge commit's message say "keep 60 s default, add a hard_mode block" instead of the default "Merge branch 'hard-mode'"?

  • The default message only says that a merge happened, not what was decided.

  • Git accepts the default message; it's just less useful.

  • The message length has no effect on what the commit stores.

Show answer

A. The default message only says that a merge happened, not what was decided.

3Which file should tell the next programmer that the game code still has to read hard_mode?

  • The CHANGELOG lists what users will notice per version, not follow-up work for developers.

  • Consequences lists what the decision makes necessary, so it's where that note belongs.

  • Commit messages stay short; the reasoning and follow-ups belong in a document people can find.

Show answer

B. Consequences lists what the decision makes necessary, so it's where that note belongs.

Key takeaways

  • Start resolving by asking what each side was trying to achieve, not which button to press.
  • When one value can't satisfy both goals, change the file's shape so each goal gets its own place.
  • Complete Merge stages the file. You still commit the merge yourself.
  • Write the resolution into the merge commit's message, and the reasons into a decision record.
  • Update the README and CHANGELOG in the same commit series as the change they describe.

#Extend it

  • Turn on the zdiff3 style for this repo only with git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3, then redo the conflict in a copy of the folder and compare the markers.
  • Push the repo to GitHub and open an issue titled "Game code must read hard_mode", linking to decision 0001.
  • Make the conflict again in a fresh copy, but this time run git rebase main on hard-mode. Notice which side the markers call HEAD.

  • Keep a Changelog (opens in a new tab): the short guide behind the CHANGELOG format used here, with the full list of section headings.
  • Documenting Architecture Decisions (opens in a new tab): Michael Nygard's original post introducing decision records, still the clearest description of why they work.

What you'll learn

  • Predict whether a merge will conflict before running it.
  • Resolve conflicts in text files, during a rebase, and when one side deleted the file.
  • Use git merge --abort and git stash -u to get out of the way safely.
  • Write a decision record that a teammate could act on.

Do each exercise in a throwaway folder (mkdir practice-5 && cd practice-5 && git init) so mistakes cost nothing. The outputs below are real; your commit IDs will differ.

#Warm-up: conflict or clean?

For each pair of changes to the same file, predict whether git merge stops.

  1. Branch A edits line 2. Branch B edits line 8.
  2. Branch A edits line 4. Branch B edits line 5.
  3. Both branches add the identical line in the same place.
  4. Branch A edits README.md. Branch B edits settings.json.
Show solution
  1. Clean: the changes are far apart, so Git takes each one.
  2. Conflict: changes on neighboring lines count as touching.
  3. Clean: when both sides made exactly the same change, there is nothing to choose.
  4. Clean: different files never conflict with each other's content.

#Exercise 1: Read the markers

You're on main and merged a branch called fix-run-command. The README now says:

Which command came from main? Write a resolved README that keeps both, since py works on Windows and python3 on macOS and Linux.

Need a hint?

HEAD is the branch you were on when you started the merge.

Show solution

py quiz.py came from main, the current branch; python3 quiz.py came in from fix-run-command. One good resolution:

Then git diff --check, git add README.md, and git commit. The best resolutions often say more than either side did alone.

#Exercise 2: Back out of a merge you didn't mean to start

You merged the wrong branch and the conflict is in a file you've never seen. Undo the merge so your folder is exactly as it was, and prove it with git status.

Need a hint?

You don't need to touch the conflicted file at all.

Show solution

--abort only works while the merge is still in progress. Once you've committed a merge, undoing it is a different, bigger job, so check which branch you're merging before you press Enter.

#Exercise 3: Stash a brand-new file too

On a branch music-round, change settings.json and create a new file music.txt without committing either. Run git stash, then git status --short. What stayed behind? Fix it so both changes are stashed, with a message you'll recognize later.

Need a hint?

Look at the ?? line. Untracked files need an extra flag.

Show solution

Plain git stash took the tracked change and left the untracked music.txt behind. Bring everything back with git stash pop, then stash again with -u and a message:

The empty line after git status --short means the folder is clean. git stash pop brings back both files.

#Exercise 4: Resolve a conflict in the middle of a rebase

Make a README with the line Teams of up to 4 players. and commit it on main. On a branch team-size, change it to Teams of 2 to 4 players. and commit. Back on main, change it to Teams of up to 5 players. and commit. Now switch to team-size and run git rebase main. Resolve so both rules survive, and finish the rebase.

Need a hint?

During a rebase the labels flip. HEAD is the branch you are replaying onto (main), and the other side is your own commit.

Show solution

The README shows main's line under HEAD and your commit under its ID:

Both rules fit in one sentence: Teams of 2 to 5 players. Write that, remove the markers, then:

Git may open your editor to confirm the commit message; save and close it. "Detached HEAD" is normal mid-rebase, and the last line tells you the branch is back on track.

#Exercise 5: One side deleted the file

On a branch tidy-up, someone ran git rm old-questions.txt because it looked unused. Meanwhile on main, you added a question to that same file. Merge tidy-up into main. Read the message, then decide: does the file stay or go?

Need a hint?

There are no markers this time. Git needs you to either git add the file (keep it) or git rm it (delete it).

Show solution

Your new question shows the file is not dead after all, so keep it with git add old-questions.txt and commit. If the game really doesn't read it, move your question to the file it does use, then git rm old-questions.txt and commit. Either is fine; what matters is that you decided on purpose and said why in the commit message.

#Exercise 6: Write the decision record

Two pull requests clashed in settings.json. One switched the default theme to "dark" because the club meets in a dim room. The other kept "light" because the projector washes out dark colors. The team agreed: keep "light" as the default and add a "projector" setting that switches to a high-contrast light theme. Write docs/decisions/0002-...md.

Need a hint?

Use the three headings from the build-along. Consequences should name at least one piece of follow-up work.

Show solution

Find the problem with one command, fix it, and write a CHANGELOG entry for the rename.

Need a hint?

Try git grep -n "seconds" after the merge.

Show solution

The merge is clean, because the two edits are several lines apart:

But the file now uses two names for the same idea:

Rename the key inside hard_mode too, commit, and add this under Unreleased in the CHANGELOG:

Git only notices clashing lines, not clashing meaning. Catching this kind of mistake is a job for automated tests, which Module 7 sets up.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what others may do with a public repo that has no license.
  • Compare MIT, Apache-2.0, and GPL-3.0, and know when a Creative Commons license fits instead.
  • Decide whether a change is a major, minor, or patch release.
  • Mark a release with an annotated Git tag and turn it into a GitHub Release.

You find a public repo with exactly the countdown timer Quiz Night needs. There's no LICENSE file. Can you copy the code into your project?

Legally, no. Without a license, normal copyright applies: the author keeps every right, and nobody may copy, change, or share the work. GitHub's terms let other users view and fork a public repo on GitHub, and that's all. Being public is not the same as being open source. One file, LICENSE, is the difference.

📝 Note

This lesson explains licenses in everyday words so you can make sensible choices for school and hobby projects. It isn't legal advice. If money, a company, or a school's rules are involved, ask someone who can give it.

#What a license actually does

A license is the author saying in advance: "You may do these things with my work, as long as you follow these conditions." Without it, every person who wants to reuse your code would have to ask you and get an answer. With it, they already know the answer.

Open-source licenses all allow using, studying, changing, and sharing. They differ mostly in their conditions: what you must do in return.

#Three software licenses in plain words

MIT Apache-2.0 GPL-3.0
Use, change, share, even sell Yes Yes Yes
Must keep the copyright and license notice Yes Yes Yes
Must mark files you changed No Yes Yes
Contributors grant patent rights in writing No Yes Yes
Shared modified versions must stay open, under the same license No No Yes

MIT is the short one, about 170 words. Do nearly anything, keep the notice, and don't sue the author if it breaks. It is the most common license on GitHub because it asks so little.

Apache-2.0 allows the same freedoms with more paperwork. Its big addition is an explicit patent grant: everyone who contributes gives users permission to use any of their patents that the contribution needs. Companies often prefer it for that reason.

GPL-3.0 is copyleft. Anyone can use and change the code, but if you distribute a modified version, or a program that includes GPL code, you must share its complete source under the GPL too. Changes you keep to yourself carry no obligation. The point is that improvements stay open for everyone.

#Licenses for things that aren't code

Quiz Night also has a question bank, artwork, and documentation. Creative Commons licenses are written for that kind of work:

  • CC BY 4.0: anyone may reuse it if they credit you.
  • CC BY-SA 4.0: credit you, and share their adapted versions under the same license.
  • CC0: you give up your rights as far as the law allows. No conditions at all.

Creative Commons itself recommends against using its licenses for software, because they say nothing about source code or patents. A project can mix: code under MIT, questions/ under CC BY 4.0. Say which is which in the README. Variants with NC (non-commercial) or ND (no derivatives) are valid licenses, but they aren't open source, since they forbid uses open source allows.

#Picking one with choosealicense.com

GitHub runs choosealicense.com (opens in a new tab), which asks what you care about and shows each license's permissions, conditions, and limitations side by side. Its page for MIT tells you exactly what to do: create a file named LICENSE, paste the text, and replace [year] and [fullname].

On GitHub you can do the same without leaving the browser: Add file › Create new file, type LICENSE as the name, click Choose a license template, pick one, and click Review and submit. Once GitHub detects the file, the license name appears in the repo's sidebar.

#Version numbers that mean something

A release name like "Quiz Night, the good one" tells users nothing. Semantic versioning (semver) uses three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and each one has a job:

  • PATCH (1.0.0 → 1.0.1): a bug fix that changes nothing anyone relies on.
  • MINOR (1.0.1 → 1.1.0): something new that doesn't break what already worked.
  • MAJOR (1.1.0 → 2.0.0): a change that can break things for existing users.

Bumping a number resets everything to its right, so the minor release after 1.4.7 is 1.5.0, not 1.5.7. Versions starting with 0, like 0.3.0, mean "still in early development; anything may change." Releasing 1.0.0 is a promise that you'll follow the rules from now on.

What counts as "breaking" depends on what users rely on. For Quiz Night, players and club leaders rely on the format of settings.json. Adding a categories list is minor, because old settings files still work. Renaming time_limit_seconds is major, because every existing settings file stops working.

Version numbers look like decimals, but they aren't, and comparing them as text gives wrong answers. Predict what each line prints, then run it:

Text comparison goes character by character, and "1" comes before "9", so "1.10.0" sorts first. Turning each part into a number compares 10 with 9 as numbers.

#Tags mark the commit, releases tell the story

A tag is a permanent name for one commit. Unlike a branch, it never moves. Releases use annotated tags, which store who made them, when, and a message:

The v is a common habit, not part of semver itself. Note the second line: git push on its own doesn't send tags, so you push each one by name.

A GitHub Release is built on a tag. It adds a title, release notes, and download links. GitHub attaches the source code as .zip and .tar.gz files automatically, and a Generate release notes button drafts notes from the merged pull requests. The next lesson walks through creating one.

⚠️ Watch out

Mistakes that cause real trouble.

  1. Publishing without a license and assuming people may reuse your work. They may not.
  2. Switching licenses later and expecting it to apply backward. People who already got a copy under the old license keep those rights, and once others have contributed, changing usually needs their agreement too.
  3. Tagging, then forgetting git push origin v1.0.0. The tag exists only on your computer, and GitHub has nothing to build a release from.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A public GitHub repo has no LICENSE file. What may you do with its code?

  • Public means visible. Without a license, copyright keeps every right with the author.

  • GitHub's terms allow viewing and forking; reuse needs the author's permission.

  • Credit is a condition some licenses add. With no license, there is no permission to attach it to.

Show answer

B. GitHub's terms allow viewing and forking; reuse needs the author's permission.

2Quiz Night 1.4.2 adds a "music" category. Old settings files still work. What's the next version?

  • Patch is for fixes. A new feature is more than a fix.

  • New, non-breaking functionality bumps minor and resets patch to 0.

  • Nothing broke, so a major bump would wrongly warn users.

Show answer

B. New, non-breaking functionality bumps minor and resets patch to 0.

3You want anyone who shares an improved version of your app to share its source too. Which license matches?

  • MIT lets people share modified versions without their source.

  • Apache-2.0 adds a patent grant, but modified versions can still be closed.

  • Its copyleft condition requires distributed modified versions to stay open under the GPL.

Show answer

C. Its copyleft condition requires distributed modified versions to stay open under the GPL.

4You ran git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Quiz Night 1.1.0" and then git push. GitHub's release page doesn't list v1.1.0. Why?

  • Run git push origin v1.1.0 to send it.

  • They can, and they are the recommended kind for releases.

  • Releases are built from tags, not from a special branch.

Show answer

A. Run git push origin v1.1.0 to send it.

Key takeaways

  • No license means all rights reserved, even on a public repo.
  • MIT asks for the notice, Apache-2.0 adds a patent grant and change notes, GPL-3.0 keeps shared modified versions open.
  • Use Creative Commons for writing, images, and data; use a software license for code.
  • MAJOR breaks things, MINOR adds things, PATCH fixes things, and bumping one resets the numbers to its right.
  • Releases get annotated tags, pushed by name, and GitHub Releases add notes and downloads on top.

What you'll learn

  • Choose the right version bump for a set of changes.
  • Write Python that bumps and sorts version numbers correctly.
  • Match a license to what an author wants.
  • Turn raw commit history into a useful CHANGELOG entry, and move a tag that landed on the wrong commit.

Exercises 2, 3, and the challenge are Python; run them right here. The Git exercises use a copy of your quiz-night folder, so the real one stays tidy: copy the folder, then work in the copy.

#Warm-up: read a version number

Python's version 3.12.4 has three parts. Which number is the patch? What would the next minor release be called?

Show solution

The patch is 4. The next minor release is 3.13.0: minor goes up by one and patch resets to 0.

#Exercise 1: Pick the next version

Quiz Night is at 2.3.1. For each change on its own, what is the next version?

  1. Fix a crash when settings.json has no theme.
  2. Add a projector option.
  3. Remove the old colour spelling that was still accepted alongside color.
  4. Correct a spelling mistake in the README.
  5. Three bug fixes and one new option, released together.
Need a hint?

Ask "could this break someone's existing settings file?" first, then "does it add anything?"

Show solution
  1. 2.3.2: a fix that breaks nothing.
  2. 2.4.0: a new feature; old settings still work.
  3. 3.0.0: settings files that say colour stop working, so it's breaking.
  4. No new version is needed for a docs-only change. If you do publish one, it's a patch.
  5. 2.4.0: the biggest kind of change in the batch decides. Fixes ride along with the feature.

#Exercise 2: Write bump()

Write bump(version, part), where part is "major", "minor", or "patch". It returns the next version as a string. Test it on 1.4.7 with all three parts, and on 0.9.9 with "minor".

Need a hint?

version.split(".") gives three strings. Convert them with int, and remember that bumping a number resets everything to its right.

Show solution

The last test is the one people get wrong on paper: after 0.9.9 comes 0.10.0, not 1.0.0. Going to 1.0.0 is a decision, not arithmetic. Raising ValueError for a typo like "mnior" is better than quietly returning the old version.

#Exercise 3: Sort release tags

git tag lists tags alphabetically, so v1.10.0 appears before v1.2.0. Write code that sorts these tags by version and prints the newest: ["v1.10.0", "v1.2.0", "v2.0.0", "v1.9.3", "v1.2.10"].

Need a hint?

Strip the v, split on dots, and turn the parts into a tuple of numbers. Tuples compare item by item.

Show solution

Git can do this too: git tag --sort=version:refname sorts tags by version instead of alphabetically.

#Exercise 4: Match the license

Which license fits each author?

  1. A robotics club wants anyone, including companies, to reuse their code with as few rules as possible.
  2. A student wants anyone who shares an improved version of her game to share its source as well.
  3. A teacher is sharing a folder of quiz questions and hand-drawn diagrams and wants credit.
Need a hint?

Only one of these is software.

Show solution
  1. MIT: keep the notice, and that's nearly all. (Apache-2.0 also works if they want the patent grant.)
  2. GPL-3.0: its copyleft condition makes distributed modified versions stay open.
  3. CC BY 4.0: questions and drawings aren't software, and CC BY requires credit. Creative Commons advises against its licenses for code, so if the folder later gains code, license that part separately.

#Exercise 5: Turn a log into a CHANGELOG entry

These commits landed after v1.1.0:

Write the CHANGELOG section for the next release, including its version number. Users read this, not developers.

Need a hint?

v1.1.0..HEAD means "commits after v1.1.0 up to now." One of these breaks existing settings files. One isn't worth mentioning to users.

Show solution

The rename forces 2.0.0, and it goes first, with instructions, because it's the change that can hurt someone. The README screenshot is left out: it doesn't change what users get. A CHANGELOG is a summary for people, not a copy of git log.

#Exercise 6: Move a tag that landed on the wrong commit

In your copy of quiz-night, you tag v1.1.0 and only then commit the CHANGELOG update. The tag now points at the commit before the release commit. Move it, then prove that release tags are annotated by comparing one with a quick lightweight tag.

Need a hint?

Delete the tag locally with git tag -d, then create it again while HEAD is on the right commit. git cat-file -t prints what kind of object a name points to.

Show solution

Now compare the two kinds of tag:

The annotated tag is its own object with a tagger, date, and message. The lightweight one is just a name pointing straight at a commit. Delete the experiment with git tag -d v1.1.0-quick.

If you had already pushed the wrong tag, you would also need git push origin --delete v1.1.0 before pushing the fixed one, and anyone who fetched it would still have the old version. Fixing a tag before you push is cheap; afterward it's awkward, which is why checking git log --oneline --decorate before pushing is a good habit.

#Challenge: sort pre-releases correctly

Projects often publish test versions like 1.0.0-beta.2 before 1.0.0. Semver's rules say a pre-release comes before its release, and pre-release parts compare one by one: numbers compare as numbers, words compare alphabetically, numbers rank below words, and fewer parts rank lower if all earlier parts match. Write semver_key(version) so this list sorts into the official order, ending with 1.0.0:

["1.0.0", "1.0.0-rc.1", "1.0.0-beta.11", "1.0.0-beta.2", "1.0.0-beta", "1.0.0-alpha.beta", "1.0.0-alpha.1", "1.0.0-alpha"]

Need a hint?

Split on the first - with partition. Give a plain release an extra 1 at position 3 and a pre-release a 0, so releases win. For each pre-release part, (0, number) or (1, word) makes numbers rank below words.

Show solution

This matches the example order in section 11 of the semver spec. beta.2 sorts before beta.11 because 2 and 11 are compared as numbers, and alpha before alpha.1 because it has fewer parts.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a GitHub Actions workflow and say when it runs and what it does.
  • Explain how a failing command becomes a red X on a pull request.
  • Use branch protection so main only accepts reviewed, passing changes.
  • Contribute to someone else's project through a fork, an upstream remote, and its CONTRIBUTING guide.
  • Keep secrets out of Git, and know what to do first if one leaks.

In one month, Quiz Night's main branch broke three times: a missing comma after a merge, a hard mode slower than normal mode, and a renamed setting that merged cleanly but broke the game. Players found each bug on Friday night. A program that runs the tests on every pull request, before anyone clicks Merge, would have caught all three in under a minute.

That program is a GitHub Actions workflow, and it's one YAML file.

#What a workflow is

A workflow is a file in your repo's .github/workflows/ folder. It says three things:

  • When to run: on events such as a push or a pull request.
  • Where to run: on a runner, a fresh virtual computer GitHub starts for each run and throws away afterward.
  • What to run: a list of steps, in order, inside a job.

If any step's command fails, the job fails, and GitHub shows a red X next to the commit and on the pull request. If every step succeeds, you get a green check.

GitHub's standard runners are free for public repositories.

#A workflow, line by line

Here is the workflow you'll add to Quiz Night in the next lesson:

  • name: Tests is how the workflow appears in the Actions tab.
  • on: lists the triggers: every push to main, and every pull request (including each new push to one).
  • jobs: holds one job with the id unittest. That id becomes part of the check's name on pull requests.
  • runs-on: ubuntu-latest asks for a Linux runner.
  • Each - under steps: is one step. A step either uses a ready-made action or runs a shell command.
  • actions/checkout copies your repo onto the runner, which starts empty. Forget it and the next steps find no files.
  • actions/setup-python installs the Python version you name under with:.
  • run: python -m unittest -v finds every file whose name starts with test and runs the tests in it.

The @v7 picks the action's major version. New majors come out every year or so and GitHub's docs sometimes lag, so check each action's README for the current number. YAML indentation must be spaces, never tabs: with: sits two spaces deeper than uses: because it belongs to that step.

#Pass or fail is just an exit code

The runner doesn't read your test output. It only checks whether each command exited with code 0, the code programs return when they succeed. python -m unittest exits with 0 when all tests pass and 1 when any fail, so anything you can check with a command can become a check: tests, a JSON validator, a spell checker.

When a run fails, click Details next to the check on the pull request (or open the Actions tab), then the red step. Its log shows the same output you'd see in your own terminal.

#Branch protection turns a check into a rule

A red X is a warning. Anyone can still click Merge. Branch protection makes it a rule. In your repo, go to Settings › Branches, click Add classic branch protection rule, type main as the Branch name pattern, and tick:

  • Require a pull request before merging, so nobody pushes straight to main.
  • Require status checks to pass before merging, then search for your job's name (unittest) and select it.

Click Create. The check's name shows up in that search box once the workflow has run at least once, so push the workflow before you make the rule. On a free account, branch protection works on public repositories. GitHub also offers rulesets under Settings › Rules, a newer way to set the same kind of rules; either works for this course.

📝 Note

By default, repository admins can bypass these rules. On your own repo, that's you. Tick Do not allow bypassing the above settings if you want the rules to apply to you too.

#Contributing to a project you don't own

You can't push branches to someone else's repository. Instead you fork it: GitHub makes a copy under your account, and you push there.

After cloning your fork, add the original as a second remote called upstream:

octocat/Spoon-Knife is GitHub's practice repo for forking. To pick up new work from the original, run git fetch upstream and git merge upstream/main, or click Sync fork on your fork's page.

Before writing code, read the project's CONTRIBUTING.md. GitHub links to it when you open an issue or pull request, and it explains that project's rules: how to run tests, how to name branches, whether to open an issue first. Look for issues labeled good first issue, which also appear on the repo's /contribute page. Comment that you'd like to take one and wait for a maintainer's reply, so two people don't fix the same thing.

#Secrets never go in Git

An API key, password, or token in a commit isn't "hidden in the history." Once pushed to a public repo it's public, and bots scan new commits for keys around the clock. Three habits prevent it:

  1. Keep secrets in a file named .env, and add .env to .gitignore before you create the file.
  2. Have your code read the value from the environment, never from a string in the source.
  3. When a workflow needs a secret, store it under Settings › Secrets and variables › Actions with New repository secret, and refer to it as ${{ secrets.WEATHER_KEY }}. GitHub hides the value in logs, and it doesn't hand secrets to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks.

GitHub helps too. Secret scanning runs automatically for free on public repositories and alerts you to known kinds of keys. Push protection for users is on by default and blocks pushes to public repositories that contain keys it recognizes.

If a key leaks anyway, the order matters:

  1. Revoke or rotate the key first, at the service that issued it. Deleting the commit doesn't help; it may already be copied.
  2. Put a new key in .env and check that .gitignore covers it.
  3. Tell whoever owns the project, so they can check for misuse.
  4. Only then decide whether to scrub the old key from history. A revoked key is useless, and rewriting history is a big job every collaborator has to repeat.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic mistakes.

  1. Saving the workflow in .github/workflow/ (no s) or using tabs. GitHub silently ignores the first and rejects the second.
  2. Requiring a check by a name that never ran, then wondering why it can't be found.
  3. Deleting the commit that leaked a key and calling it fixed. Revoke the key.
  4. Opening a big pull request on a project you've never talked to. Ask in the issue first.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A teammate pushes a new commit to a branch with an open pull request. With the workflow above, what happens?

  • The pull_request trigger fires on each new push to an open pull request.

  • branches: [main] limits the push trigger. The pull_request trigger has no such limit here.

  • That would be too late to catch the bug; pull request checks run before merging.

Show answer

A. The pull_request trigger fires on each new push to an open pull request.

2The tests pass on your laptop, but on GitHub the test step prints Ran 0 tests and NO TESTS RAN, and the job fails. Which step is most likely missing?

  • Python clearly ran, since it printed a result. The problem is what it found.

  • The runner starts empty, so unittest found no test files. Checkout is what copies your files onto it.

  • The workflow name is a label. It doesn't affect what runs.

Show answer

B. The runner starts empty, so unittest found no test files. Checkout is what copies your files onto it.

3You find a good first issue in a project you've never contributed to. What should you do first?

  • Unrelated changes make review hard. Keep the change small and about the issue.

  • It tells you the project's rules and stops two people from doing the same work.

  • You can't push to a repo you don't have write access to; that's what forks are for.

Show answer

B. It tells you the project's rules and stops two people from doing the same work.

4You pushed a commit containing a real API key to a public repo. What comes first?

  • The key may already be copied, so it would still work for whoever has it.

  • Copies made while it was public still exist, and the key still works.

  • A revoked key is useless to anyone who copied it. Cleanup comes after.

Show answer

C. A revoked key is useless to anyone who copied it. Cleanup comes after.

Key takeaways

  • A workflow lives in .github/workflows/, runs on events, and fails when any step's command exits with a non-zero code.
  • actions/checkout comes first, because a runner starts with no files.
  • Branch protection with required status checks turns "please run the tests" into a rule.
  • Contribute through a fork: origin is your copy, upstream is the original, and CONTRIBUTING.md is the rulebook.
  • Secrets live in .env (ignored) or in GitHub's Actions secrets. If one leaks, revoke it before anything else.

#Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Building and testing Python (opens in a new tab): official examples for testing on several Python versions and installing dependencies.
  • Open Source Guides: How to Contribute (opens in a new tab): finding a project, reading its signals, and communicating well with maintainers.
  • GitHub Docs: Push protection (opens in a new tab): what push protection blocks and what happens when it does.

3 questions

1Why push a deliberately broken commit in Step 7?

  • A check that can't go red protects nothing. Seeing it fail once builds trust in the green.

  • A check needs to have run once, but it doesn't have to have failed.

  • The revert keeps history honest, but length was never the goal.

2Why fix the slower hard mode with git revert instead of deleting the commit?

Key takeaways

  • git revert undoes a pushed commit safely; branch protection makes the passing check required.

#Extend it

  • Test on several Python versions by adding a strategy: with matrix: python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"] and using ${{ matrix.python-version }} in the setup step.
  • Add a status badge: in the Actions tab, open the Tests workflow, use the ... menu to pick Create status badge, and paste the Markdown at the top of your README.
  • Add a test that fails if categories is empty, then open a pull request that empties it and watch the check catch it.

  • GitHub Docs: Quickstart for GitHub Actions (opens in a new tab): a minimal workflow and a tour of the Actions tab.
  • GitHub Docs: Workflow syntax (opens in a new tab): every key you can use in a workflow file, including on, jobs, and strategy.
  • GitHub Docs: Managing a branch protection rule (opens in a new tab): the full list of protection options and what each one does.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read and fix GitHub Actions workflow files.
  • Run one job on several Python versions with a matrix.
  • Set up origin and upstream for a fork and sync with the original.
  • Load secrets from the environment and respond to a leaked key in the right order.
  • Write a CONTRIBUTING guide a newcomer could follow.

Use your quiz-night repo for the workflow exercises. Each change goes on its own branch with a pull request, so you see every check's result on GitHub.

#Warm-up: when does this run?

When does a workflow with this on: block start?

Show solution

On pull requests that target main, and whenever someone starts it by hand: workflow_dispatch adds a Run workflow button to the workflow's page in the Actions tab. It does not run on plain pushes, not even pushes to main.

#Exercise 1: Fix the broken workflow

This workflow has three bugs. Find them before reading the hint.

Need a hint?

One step is missing entirely. One line is at the wrong depth. One keyword is wrong for running a shell command.

Show solution
  1. There's no actions/checkout step, so the runner has no files and unittest finds no tests.
  2. python-version is at the same depth as with:, so YAML reads with: as empty and python-version as a stray key on the step. GitHub rejects the file as invalid.
  3. uses: is for ready-made actions. A shell command needs run:.

on: [push, pull_request] is a valid short form. It runs on pushes to every branch, so a pull request's branch gets checked twice: once for the push and once for the pull request. Limiting push to main, as in the build-along, avoids the duplicate.

#Exercise 2: Test on three Python versions

Club members run Quiz Night on Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13. Change the workflow so the tests run on all three, and add a step that checks settings.json is valid JSON before the tests run, so a broken file gets its own clear failure.

Need a hint?

Add strategy: with a matrix: under the job, then refer to the value as ${{ matrix.python-version }}. For the JSON step, python -m json.tool settings.json exits with an error code when the file is invalid.

Show solution

GitHub now runs three copies of the job at the same time, one per version, and the pull request shows three checks with the version in each name. Put the versions in quotes: unquoted, YAML reads 3.10 as the number 3.1.

If you required unittest in branch protection, update the rule: the old check name no longer appears, and the three new names do.

#Exercise 3: Set up a fork's remotes

Fork GitHub's practice repo octocat/Spoon-Knife (opens in a new tab) with the Fork button, clone your fork, add the original as upstream, and sync your main with it.

Need a hint?

After cloning, origin already points at your fork. You add upstream yourself.

Show solution

"Already up to date" is expected for a fresh fork. On an active project, run the last two commands before starting each new branch, so you build on the newest code and meet fewer conflicts later.

#Exercise 4: Read a key from the environment

Write Python that reads QUIZ_API_KEY from the environment. If it's missing, print a helpful message instead of crashing. If it's there, print only its last four characters, so the key never appears in full in a log.

Need a hint?

os.environ.get(name) returns None when the variable isn't set.

Show solution

It isn't set on this page, so you see the friendly message. On your computer, the popular python-dotenv package can load .env into the environment for you. In a workflow, pass a repository secret into the same variable:

The code doesn't change between your laptop and GitHub. Only where the value comes from does.

#Exercise 5: A key leaked. Put the response in order

You pushed config.py with a real key in it to a public repo an hour ago. Put these in order and cross out the one that doesn't help:

  • A. Move the key into .env, add .env to .gitignore, and read it with os.environ.
  • B. Revoke the key at the service and create a new one.
  • C. Tell the project owner or your teacher what happened.
  • D. Make the repository private and consider the problem solved.
  • E. Decide whether to scrub the old key from history.
Need a hint?

What can someone do with the key right now, while you're still editing files?

Show solution

B, A, C, E. Revoking comes first, because until then anyone who copied the key can use it. Then fix the code so the new key never lands in Git. Then tell the owner, who may need to check for misuse. History cleanup comes last and is optional once the old key is dead.

D doesn't help. Copies made while the repo was public still exist, and the key still works until you revoke it.

#Exercise 6: Spot the unsafe workflow

A classmate's workflow prints debugging info. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?

Need a hint?

Where does this text live, and who can read it?

Show solution

The key is typed straight into the workflow file, so it's in the repo's history for anyone to read, and it's printed in every run's log. Revoke that key, store a new one as a repository secret, pass it in with env: as in Exercise 4, and never echo it. GitHub masks registered secrets in logs, but it can't mask a value it was never told is secret.

#Challenge: write CONTRIBUTING.md

Write a CONTRIBUTING.md for Quiz Night that a classmate who has never seen the repo could follow from fork to merged pull request. Include: how to set up and run the tests, how to name branches, what a good pull request contains, and one rule about secrets.

Need a hint?

Write it as numbered steps. A newcomer should never have to guess the next command.

Show solution

GitHub links to this file when someone opens an issue or a pull request, so put the most important rules near the top.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe every stage of a contribution, from issue to merged pull request.
  • Choose a capstone project that matches your skills and time.
  • Follow the safety and etiquette rules for public repositories.
  • Write a plan with a claimed issue, a branch name, a test plan, and milestones.

A stranger opens a pull request on your repo that fixes a typo in the README. It's six characters, and it involves almost everything in this course: an issue, a fork, a branch, a commit, a pull request, an automated check, a review, maybe a conflict, and a merge. Small contributions like that keep open source running.

Your capstone is to make one such contribution, carefully, and show the evidence for every step.

#The brief

Take one change all the way from an issue to a merged pull request (or, on the solo track, a pull request you merge yourself). Along the way you must:

  1. Claim an issue that describes the change, or write one.
  2. Work on a branch in a fork (or in your own repo on the solo track).
  3. Make focused commits with messages that say what and why.
  4. Open a pull request that links the issue and explains how you tested.
  5. Respond to review with at least one follow-up commit and a reply.
  6. Sync with the latest main before merging, and resolve any conflict without losing anyone's work.
  7. Update documentation: the README, the CHANGELOG, or a decision record, whichever fits.
  8. Pass an automated check: the project's own, or one you add.

You'll hand in three things: a link to the pull request (or screenshots, if it's private), the output of git log --oneline --graph for your branch, and a short reflection, covered in the last lesson.

#Pick a project at your level

Track What you do Where Good for
1. Solo rehearsal Write an issue for yourself, fix it on a branch, open a PR, review your own diff, rehearse a conflict by editing main on GitHub first Your quiz-night repo Working alone, or under 13 with an adult's account
2. Partner swap Each of you forks the other's repo and fixes an issue its owner wrote; each owner reviews A classmate's repo from this course Classes and clubs
3. First Contributions Add your name to a contributors list through a fork firstcontributions/first-contributions (opens in a new tab) A real public PR with very little risk
4. Real project Fix a good first issue, often in documentation A project you actually use Confident learners with time to wait for replies
5. Maintainer track Make your repo contributor-ready (CONTRIBUTING, branch protection, CI, a release), then review and merge a friend's PR Your quiz-night repo Anyone who wants to run a project

Track 3 is a project built for first pull requests, and its README walks you through the steps. So many people edit the same file that your branch often falls behind while you work, which makes it good practice for syncing with upstream.

Track 4 needs the most patience. Maintainers are usually volunteers, and a reply can take days. Pick an issue that's still open, has no one assigned, and hasn't been claimed in the comments.

#Rules for working in public

  • Age: GitHub accounts are for people 13 and older. Younger learners do track 1 with an adult or teacher's help.
  • Privacy: issues, comments, and commits on public repos are visible to everyone, forever. Don't include your full name, school, address, or phone number. Use the private noreply commit email from Module 1.
  • Secrets: never paste a key, password, or token into code, an issue, or a screenshot.
  • Respect: read and follow the project's code of conduct. Assume good intent, and thank reviewers even when they ask for changes.
  • Ask first: comment on the issue and wait for a maintainer to say yes before you spend hours on it.
  • No spam: pull requests that change one space just to get a contribution count waste maintainers' time, and some projects block accounts that send them.
  • Understand every line: if a tool or a friend wrote part of your change, you must still be able to explain it in review. If you can't, don't submit it.

#Your plan

Copy this into a file called PLAN.md on your computer (not in the project you're contributing to) and fill in every line before you write any code:

For a partner swap, write each other's issues first. A good issue describes the problem and what "done" looks like, without dictating the fix: "The README doesn't say how to run the tests. Done when a newcomer can run them by following the README alone."

#Milestones and timing

Track 1 fits in two or three sessions. Track 4 can take longer, because M5 depends on someone else's schedule; start your reflection while you wait.

💡 Tip

Choose a smaller change than you think you need. A typo fix that goes through every step teaches more than a big feature that never gets reviewed.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone is one small change taken through every stage: issue, branch, commits, pull request, review, sync, docs, and a passing check.
  • Pick the track that matches your time; a finished small contribution beats an unfinished big one.
  • Public means permanent: no personal details, no secrets, and respect for the code of conduct.
  • Claim the issue and wait for a yes before you start.
