m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Set up a fork with origin and upstream, and branch from the newest code.
  • Make, test, and push a focused change, then open a pull request that links its issue.
  • Sync with upstream when main moves, and resolve the conflict so both changes survive.
  • Answer review with a follow-up commit, and check exactly what your pull request contains.

This lesson follows one real contribution from start to finish, so you can compare each step with your own. Maya owns the original quiz-night repo (the upstream). You fork it and fix her issue #3: "The README doesn't say how to run the tests." Here is the branch at the end, ready to merge:

Read it from the bottom. You branched from Maya's latest main, made your change, merged in a change she made meanwhile, and added a commit her review asked for.

#Starter kit

On tracks 1, 2, and 5 you contribute to a quiz-night repo built in Modules 5 to 7. If yours is missing pieces, add them from those lessons: settings.json, quiz.py, test_quiz.py, README.md, CHANGELOG.md, LICENSE, and .github/workflows/tests.yml. On tracks 3 and 4, the project you picked is your starter.

Whoever owns the repo should also add a pull request template. GitHub pre-fills every new pull request's description with it:

#Milestone 1: Claim the issue

On the issue, write a short comment and wait for a reply before you start:

That one comment lets the maintainer correct your plan before you write anything, and it tells other contributors the issue is taken. Note the issue number; you'll need it in Milestone 4.

#Milestone 2: Fork, clone, connect upstream

Click Fork on the upstream repo, keep the default name, and create the fork. Then clone your fork, not the original:

git remote -v should list four lines: origin twice, pointing at your account, and upstream twice, pointing at the original. If origin points at the original, you cloned the wrong one; clone your fork into a fresh folder.

On track 1 there's no fork. Work in your own clone, and treat origin as the upstream.

#Milestone 3: Branch, change, test, commit

Name the branch after the change, not after yourself:

Add a section to the README, just above ## License:

Before committing, check the size of your change and follow your own instructions exactly as a newcomer would:

One file, eight lines, one purpose. That's a pull request anyone can review in two minutes. (The test output is the same four ok lines from Module 7.)

#Milestone 4: Push and open the pull request

On GitHub, click Compare & pull request. Check the bar at the top: the base repository must be Maya's repo with base main, and the head repository must be your fork with docs/run-tests. Fill in the template:

Fixes #3 is a linking keyword: when the pull request is merged into the default branch, GitHub closes issue #3 automatically. Within a minute, the Tests check appears at the bottom of the page and should turn green.

#Milestone 5: Main moved, so sync and resolve

While you waited, Maya merged her own change, and your pull request now says the branch has conflicts that must be resolved. Bring her work into your branch on your computer:

You both added a section in the same spot. Neither should disappear, and requirements make sense before instructions, so put Maya's section first and yours after it. Remove the markers, then verify before committing:

git push updates the pull request, and the conflict warning disappears. Merging upstream/main into your branch, rather than rebasing, keeps every commit reviewers have already seen, so you never need to force-push. If a project's CONTRIBUTING asks for rebasing instead, follow it.

#Milestone 6: Answer the review

Maya reviews and comments: "Looks great. Could you add the Windows command too? python often isn't found there." Make the change as a new commit:

Then reply to her comment so she knows it's done: "Added in 030ad30, thanks for catching that." Linking the commit lets her check it in one click. Leave Resolve conversation to the reviewer unless the project says otherwise.

Before asking for a final look, check exactly what your pull request will add to upstream:

Three commits, all about issue #3. If anything unrelated shows up here, it would show up in the pull request too.

#Milestone 7: Docs, check, merge

Your change is a documentation update, so the README is covered. It doesn't change what players see, so it doesn't need a CHANGELOG line here; follow the project's own rule if it has one. Confirm the Tests check is green on the latest commit. When the maintainer merges, issue #3 closes itself. Then tidy up your own copy:

If the project squash-merges pull requests, your exact commits never reach main, so Git may warn about the delete or refuse it. Once GitHub shows the pull request as merged, git branch -D docs/run-tests is safe.

On the maintainer track (5), you are Maya: review the pull request in the Files changed tab, leave a comment, wait for the follow-up, and merge. Then add the change to the CHANGELOG's Unreleased section if it affects users, and tag a release when you have enough for one.

⚠️ Watch out

The problems contributors hit most, and the fixes.

  • Permission denied on push: you pushed to upstream. Push to origin, your fork.
  • The pull request shows dozens of unrelated commits: you branched from an old main. Make a fresh branch from upstream/main and move your change onto it.
  • The check is red but tests pass for you: click Details and read the failing step. A missing file you forgot to git add is the usual cause.
  • No reply after several days: leave one polite follow-up comment. If there's still nothing, your work is still done and your evidence still counts.

#Hand-in checklist

  • Link to the pull request, or screenshots of it.
  • git log --oneline --graph for your branch.
  • Your filled-in PLAN.md.
  • Notes for your reflection: what surprised you, and what you'd do differently. The next lesson turns them into a write-up.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a test plan that proves your pull request contains only what it should.
  • Polish a pull request title, description, and commit history so a stranger can review it.
  • Present your contribution as a short story: problem, change, process, lesson.
  • Assess your work against the rubric and plan your next contribution.

A pull request can be merged and still be hard to understand: a title that says "Update", a description that's empty, a stray debug file. A maintainer reading your work next year and a teacher grading it now look at the same things. This lesson is the final pass before you call the capstone done.

#Run the test plan

Do every check on the latest commit of your branch. The outputs here come from the worked example in the previous lesson.

What to check How Passes when
Tests pass locally python -m unittest -v Every test says ok
The automated check is green The checks area at the bottom of the pull request Green check on the newest commit, not an older one
No leftover conflict markers git diff --check upstream/main Prints nothing
Only the files you meant to change git diff --stat upstream/main Every file listed belongs to the issue
Every commit is on topic git log --oneline upstream/main..HEAD Each message relates to the issue
No secrets git grep -n -i -E "api_key|token|password|secret" Every hit is harmless
Your docs work Follow your own README in a fresh clone You never have to guess a step
The issue is linked The pull request description It says Fixes #N and the issue shows the link

Three of these, run on the example branch:

The first command printed nothing, so no markers survived. The second shows exactly one file, which matches the issue. The search found one hit, and reading it shows it's a comment in .gitignore, not a key. That's the point of the secrets check: a tool finds candidates, and you read each one.

The "fresh clone" test catches the most embarrassing bug in documentation changes: instructions that only work on the author's computer. Clone the branch into a new folder, follow the README word for word, and fix whatever you had to work out on your own.

#Polish what reviewers read first

Reviewers see the title, then the description, then the commits. Make each one carry its weight.

Hard to review Easy to review
Title Update README Explain how to run the tests in the README
Description (empty) What, why, Fixes #3, how you tested
Commits fix, more fixes, oops Explain how to run the tests in the README

Change a pull request's title any time with Edit next to it. Answer every review comment, even if only with "Done in 030ad30". If the project's CONTRIBUTING asks for tidy history, ask the maintainer before rewriting commits on an open pull request; many projects squash everything into one commit when they merge, so a few small commits are usually fine.

#Present it in three minutes

You'll present to your class, a club, or your instructor. Tell it as a story with five beats, and show one artifact for each:

  1. The problem (show the issue): "New contributors couldn't tell how to run the tests."
  2. The change (show the Files changed tab): "I added one README section with the exact command."
  3. The process (show the graph below): "I branched from the latest main, opened a PR, and the tests ran on it automatically."
  4. What went wrong (point at the merge commit): "Maya added a section in the same spot while I worked. I merged upstream/main and kept both sections."
  5. What I learned: one sentence you couldn't have said before the course.

The graph is your best visual. Every beat of the story is visible in it: where you started, the parallel change, the merge, and the review fix.

#Write your reflection

Keep it to one page in a file called REFLECTION.md, next to your PLAN.md. Answer honestly; "I got stuck for an hour on the wrong remote" is more useful than "everything went well."

#The rubric

Criterion Beginning Developing Strong
Issue and plan No issue, or plan left mostly blank Issue exists; plan partly filled in Clear issue with a "done when"; complete plan, claimed before starting
Branch and commits Work committed on main Branch used; some vague messages Well-named branch; each commit focused, with a message saying what and why
Pull request No description Description present but missing testing or issue link What, why, Fixes #N, and how it was tested
Review response Comments ignored Changes made without replies Every comment answered, with follow-up commits linked
Sync and conflicts Branch far behind main, or someone's work lost Synced, but resolution dropped part of a change Synced with upstream; conflict resolved keeping both intentions, explained in the merge message
Documentation None README or CHANGELOG touched but unclear Docs updated so a newcomer can follow them; CHANGELOG or decision record where it fits
Automated check No check runs Check runs but was red when merged, or ignored Green check on the final commit; on track 5, a required check
Safety and etiquette Personal details or secrets exposed Minor slips, fixed when pointed out No personal data or secrets; followed CONTRIBUTING and the code of conduct
Reflection and presentation Missing Describes what happened Explains decisions and lessons, and the three-minute story is clear

A "Strong" in every row on a typo fix beats "Developing" on a big feature. The rubric grades the process, not the size of the change.

#Keep contributing

  • Practice with GitHub Skills (opens in a new tab), free interactive courses that run inside real repositories, and the free Pro Git book (opens in a new tab), especially the branching chapter.
  • Contribute by browsing github.com/topics/good-first-issue (opens in a new tab) or the /contribute page of a project you already use. Documentation fixes are almost always welcome and are a good way to learn a codebase.
  • Maintain your own project. Give quiz-night a CONTRIBUTING file, a pull request template, a required check, and a release, then invite a friend to send a pull request. Reviewing someone else's change teaches as much as writing your own.

💡 Tip

Keep a short list of every contribution you make: the link, what it changed, and one thing you learned. After a year it shows exactly what you can do.

Key takeaways

  • Prove a pull request is clean with commands: tests, git diff --check, git diff --stat, the commit list, and a search for secrets.
  • Titles, descriptions, and commit messages are written for a reviewer who has never seen your work.
  • Present a contribution as a story, and use git log --graph to show it.
  • The rubric rewards careful process over big changes.

#Further reading

  • Open Source Guides: How to Contribute (opens in a new tab): the "Anatomy of an open source project" section explains the roles you'll meet in real projects.
  • GitHub Docs: Finding ways to contribute to open source (opens in a new tab): topics pages, labels, and other ways to find a first issue.
  • Pro Git (opens in a new tab): the free book on Git, from first commit to how Git stores data.
